comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **FP8 — final write-up. Status: PARKED** (best gain ≈ +6% at d1024/d1280; not worth the complexity for now). Branch `fast-track-fp8` (local; all FP8 flags default off, BF16 unchanged, tests + lint clean).

## Bottom line
- **Quality:** every FP8 config run to the full d512 budget matched BF16 within noise (baseline 4-seed mean 3.1592, σ≈0.004).
- **Speed:** the only real win is **FP8 on the MoE all-to-all transport** (`--moe-transport fp8_dispatch_grad`: per-token E4M3 dispatch + FP8 combine output-gradient): **+3.0% d512, +5.9% d1024, +5.7% d1280**.
- **FP8 matmuls never paid through XLA**: row-wise FP8 GEMMs (dense and/or routed experts) were slower at every size; tensor-wise FP8 dense projections were ≈neutral on top of the transport win.

## Where step time goes (XProf, GPU-0 kernel ms/step)
| bucket | d512 (240 ms) | d1024 (1713 ms) | d1280 (2225 ms) |
|---|---|---|---|
| routed-expert GEMMs | 13.8 (5.8%) | 148.5 (8.7%) | 232.1 (10.4%) |
| shared-expert GEMMs | 6.8 | 79.1 | 142.9 (6.4%) |
| attention q/k/v/o GEMMs | 4.2 | 52.2 | 89.1 (4.0%) |
| router + latent GEMMs | 2.5 | 26.2 | 43.1 |
| lm_head (fused CE, kept BF16) | 7.2 | 24.9 | 32.0 |
| **MoE all-to-all** | **44.7 (18.7%)** | **303.7 (17.7%)** | **418.6 (18.8%)** |
| attention core (FA4) | 16.0 | 136.7 | 201.1 |
| unscoped / optimizer / misc | ~103 (43%) | ~515 | ~700 (31%) |

FP8-eligible GEMMs are ~11% of the d512 step (ceiling ≈6% even at a perfect 2×) and memory-bound at d512 shapes; ~22% at d1280. Non-FP8 hotspots worth more than FP8 at d512: the embedding-gradient scatter-add (~14.7 ms/step, ~6%), two MoE argsorts (~6 ms each), a 13 ms transpose fusion; the d512 all-to-all runs at an effective ~35 GB/s (latency/skew-bound).

## What was implemented
- `lib/levanter/grug/fp8.py`: power-of-2, current (just-in-time) scales. **Row-wise** (per-token activations × per-output-column / per-expert weights, E4M3, scales applied after the GEMM; FP8 dgrad with `Precision.HIGHEST`, wgrad BF16) and **tensor-wise** (`FP8_TENSOR`, `FP8_TENSOR_FWD`: per-operand scale folded into the cuBLASLt FP8 GEMM). **Bound scale** for GatedNorm(RMSNorm) inputs = `sqrt(D)·max|norm weight|` (no amax pass). XLA 0.11 gotcha: `convert(f8)*scale` is *not* rewritten to an FP8 GEMM — FP8 operands must reach `dot_general` directly.
- `MoeTransport` (grug MoE EP all-to-all): `fp8_dispatch` (per-token E4M3 + int8 exponent in a 16-byte metadata column; straight-through backward) and `fp8_dispatch_grad` (+ FP8 combine output-gradient). Two per-assignment-quantized variants (FP8 combine / FP8 all) lost at d512 and d1024 and were removed.
- Flags: `--fp8-matmuls {off,dense,experts,all}`, `--fp8-dense-scaling {fp8_rowwise,fp8_tensor,fp8_tensor_fwd}`, `--moe-transport {bf16,fp8_dispatch,fp8_dispatch_grad}`, `--profile-steps`, `--seed`. Kept BF16/FP32: embedding, lm_head/CE (per request: no FP8 lm_head), router, norms, attention core, convs, optimizer.
- Bug fixed: dropless eval swapped in a local MoE backend and crashed at the step-1191 eval with FP8 formats on; now resets them (regression test added).

## Numerics tests (CPU)
Power-of-2 scale tight and 0/inf/NaN-safe; row-wise scales independent; requantize lossless; row×column rescale exactly equals a dequantized reference (fwd + grads, dense + batched); ~3.8% error vs BF16 (E4M3 rounding); tensor-wise saturates rather than NaN when a bound is exceeded; FP8 dispatch / dispatch-grad bit-exact vs BF16 on fake-quantized inputs across 11 binades; 8-device CPU model grad rel-error vs BF16 0.18% (dispatch), ~0.6% (all matmuls FP8).

## Throughput vs same-cluster BF16 (cw-rno2a probes; median of steady-state steps)
| config | d512 ex/s | Δ | d1024 ex/s | Δ | d1280 ex/s | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| BF16 baseline | 569.9 (3 runs) | – | 187.4 (2) | – | 125.0 (2) | – |
| fp8_dispatch | 580.7 (3) | +1.9% | 192.8 | +2.9% | – | – |
| **fp8_dispatch_grad** | **586.8 (3)** | **+3.0%** | **198.5 (2)** | **+5.9%** | **132.1 (2)** | **+5.7%** |
| dense row-wise (no transport) | | −5.6%* | | −1.9%* | | |
| experts row-wise (no transport) | | −3.6%* | | | | |
| all row-wise (no transport) | | −8.4%* | | −7.5%* | | |
| dense row-wise + dgrad | – | | 191.5 | +2.2% | 130.4 | +4.3% |
| experts row-wise + dgrad | – | | – | | 125.5 | +0.4% |
| all row-wise + dgrad | – | | – | | 123.7 | −1.0% |
| dense tensor + dgrad | 570.0 | 0.0% | 194.7 | +3.9% | 132.3 | +5.8% |
| dense tensor-fwd + dgrad | 571.9 | +0.4% | 196.5 | +4.9% | 132.4 | +5.9% |
| dense tensor, global amax (reverted) | | | | | 129–131 | +3–4.6% |
| dense tensor + fused qkv/gate-up (reverted) | | | | | 130–131 | +4–4.5% |
\* single 40-step probes (short-probe baseline 574.7). Any dense/expert FP8 on top of dgrad is neutral (tensor-wise) or slower (row-wise).

## d512 loss (cw-us-east-02a, 2384 steps, data-matched)
| run | config | mid (1191) | final Paloma macro |
|---|---|---|---|
| [fasttrack-moe-d512](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/fasttrack-moe-d512) | baseline | 3.4588 | 3.1559 (4-seed mean 3.1592) |
| [fp8-d512-disp-v2](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/fp8-d512-disp-v2) | fp8_dispatch | 3.4605 | 3.1552 |
| [fp8-d512-dgrad-v2](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/fp8-d512-dgrad-v2) | fp8_dispatch_grad | 3.4595 | 3.1540 |
| [fp8-d512-dgrad-s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/fp8-d512-dgrad-s1) | fp8_dispatch_grad, seed 1 | 3.4552 | 3.1612 |
| [fp8-d512-allmm-dgrad](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/fp8-d512-allmm-dgrad) | all matmuls row-wise + dispatch_grad | 3.4599 | 3.1577 |
All within ~1σ. (`fp8-d512-disp/-alldisp/-dgrad` without `-v2` crashed at eval from the bug above; `fp8-d1280-dgrad` was cancelled when parking.)

## Why FP8 matmuls didn't pay
- d512 GEMMs are memory-bound (K=256/512): even pre-quantized FP8 is only 1.07–1.13× (1.54×/1.67× on q/o at d1024/d1280).
- XLA's Triton path runs the batched expert GEMMs at ~0.92–1.01× in FP8 — no speedup.
- Quantization passes don't fuse in XLA: at d1280 tensor-wise FP8 saved ~80 ms/step of dense GEMM time but added ~80 ms of casts/reductions/weight quantization; `shard_map` blocks fusing the cast into the norm, and removing it adds a global amax all-reduce (−1%).
- Fused qkv/gate-up GEMMs added a ~57 ms/step backward concatenate; FP8 dgrad needs an amax pass over the gradient; per-assignment all-to-all quantization (~9× rows) costs more than it saves.

## What it would take (if revisited)
- modded-nanogpt-style fused kernels: per-tensor scales with the cast fused into the producing norm/activation kernel (next-step amax as a side output, i.e. delayed scaling with headroom), weights quantized once per step after the optimizer, scales inside the GEMM — Triton/CuTe kernels in JAX (e.g. QuACK `norm_act_mod` / `gemm_epilogue`) plus delayed-scale state in the train state.
- A real SM90 FP8 expert GEMM with row/column scales in the epilogue (QuACK `GemmSm90` supports FP8 k-major), ideally with SwiGLU fused — only pays at d1024+.
- Cheaper non-FP8 wins first: embedding-gradient scatter (~6% at d512), MoE argsorts, all-to-all skew.

Commits (`fast-track-fp8`, local): `7cddca944e` row-wise FP8 + FP8 dispatch · `4062ad5ccd` --seed · `e59fab8e51` MoeTransport · `28a1b4da1a` fp8_dispatch_grad · `69115b8443` dropless-eval fix · `fe867e6b0f` prune losing transports + docs · `5c966673e4` tensor-wise dense FP8 · `470070338c` keep per-shard tensor-wise.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **KMA (KDA + MLA/Inkling + AttnRes) d512 tuning — final (Track A quality: 7 batches / 74 runs; Track B identical-math speed).** Branch `fast-track-kma-tune` (local, on top of `684b4c31d2`).

## Headline
- **Quality:** best config **B = 3.1039 ± 0.0027 (5 seeds)** vs KMA reference 3.1138 ± 0.0029 (5 seeds; −0.0099, ~4σ) and the no-feature baseline 3.1592 (**−0.055**).
- **Speed (identical math):** KMA d512 **469.6 → 691.2 ex/s (+47%)**, MFU 6.72 → 9.89 — now faster than the no-feature baseline (~570 on the same cluster). Two opt-in extras reach 749.8 ex/s (+60%).
- Caveat for fair comparison: several speedups are generic (bucketed Newton–Schulz, CE vocab tile, fused MoE input projections, sort-based MoE ranks, gather-based expand backward) and would also speed up the baseline; the AttnRes SAVE backward and merged stacks are KMA-specific.

**B flags:**
```
--local-mixer kda --kda-dt-range 0.02,0.5 --kda-gate-opt adam --kda-beta-opt muonh --kda-beta-lr-mult 2 \
--mla --mla-q-latent-div 2 --inkling-relpos --rel-extent 4096 --no-qk-norm --qk-mult 1.6 \
--rel-r-proj-opt adam --rel-proj-opt adam \
--attn-res --attn-res-num-blocks 8 --attn-res-query-lr-scale 0.1 --opt-set beta2=0.98
```
(learnable AttnRes key norm = `--attn-res-frozen-key-norm` omitted). B per-seed finals: 3.1018 / 3.1056 / 3.1077 / 3.1033 / 3.1013. Noise: 5 KMA ref seeds span 3.1095–3.1168; same-seed replicates differ by up to 0.005 (non-deterministic reductions) → single-run gaps < ~0.006 are noise.

## Multi-seed means
| config | seeds | final mean | Δ vs KMA 3.1138 | ex/s |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| KMA reference | 5 | 3.1138 | 0 | 458 old / ~630 fast build |
| COMBO: extent 2048 + qk_mult 1.3 + β2 0.99 + KDA dt 0.02–0.5 | 4 | 3.1096 | −0.004 | ~640 |
| A: COMBO + qk 1.6 + β2 0.98 + extent 4096 | 3 (+1 replicate) | 3.1068 | −0.007 | ~625 |
| **B: A + learnable key norm + KDA beta LR 2×** | **5** | **3.1039** | **−0.0099** | ~630 |
| split AttnRes q/kv queries | 2 | 3.1152 | +0.001 | −4% |
| split, kv first-half, KDA write gates from q | 2 | 3.1150 | +0.001 | −6% |
| Full AttnRes (every sublayer a source) | 2 | 3.1188 | +0.005 | ~same |
| learnable key norm alone | 2 | 3.1127 | −0.001 | – |
| β2 0.99 alone | 2 | 3.1105 | −0.003 | – |
| extent 2048 alone | 2 | 3.1116 | −0.002 | – |
| qk 1.3 alone | 2 | 3.1120 | −0.002 | – |
| dt 0.02–0.5 alone | 2 | 3.1124 | −0.001 | – |

## What mattered
- **KDA:** small help from dt 0.02–0.5 and beta LR 2× (MuonH, in combination). Neutral: gate rank 64/256, dt 0.01–1.0, dt 0.03–0.5. Worse: beta scale 2 (+0.010), dt 0.005 (+0.006), dt 0.05 (+0.007), qkvo LR 0.7× (+0.004).
- **MLA/Inkling:** qk_mult (QK-norm off) is the strongest knob (0.7 +0.006, 1.3 −0.002, 1.6 −0.005; 2.0 +0.008 alone, fine inside B). Inkling extent 2048/4096 slightly helps (global layers see 4096 context). Neutral: Inkling LR 2×. Worse: KV latent 256 (+0.009), full-rank Q (+0.010). rel_dim 32 hung at step 0 (cancelled, not investigated).
- **⚠️ MLA absorbability:** the MLA global layers still apply the fast_track **K ShortConv** (depthwise causal conv over time on k, after W_UK). k stays linear in the KV latents but each channel mixes 4 positions, so inference absorption would need one absorbed query per conv lag rather than a single W_UK absorption. Removing it (strict form, `--model-set sconv_sites=attn,mlp`) costs **+0.020**.
- **AttnRes:** one block per layer (N ≥ 6 at L=6) is best; N=3 +0.005; Full AttnRes +0.005 (2 seeds); query LR 0.1× confirmed (0.3× +0.011); learnable key norm ≈ neutral alone, kept in B. **Split q/kv queries** (both variants + q-gate ablation, 2 seeds each, and inside COMBO): no gain, 4–6% slower.
- **Global:** LR 0.8×/1.25× worse (+0.009); 0.9×/1.1× neutral inside COMBO. Adam β2 (heuristic 0.996): 0.99/0.98 better (−0.003), 0.95 inside B −0.004 (1 seed), 0.999 worse (+0.008).

## Track B — identical-math speedups (cw-rno2a, vs same-cluster refs)
| change | parity evidence | ex/s |
|---|---|---|
| AttnRes SAVE backward (keep residuals instead of per-layer recompute; d512 default; peak 11.6 → 33 GiB) | CPU grad parity < 1e-4; 400-step loss pair | 473.6 → 573.9 (+21%) |
| one parameter stack per mixer kind under AttnRes (4 → 2) | tests | → 604.2 (+5%) |
| bucketed Newton–Schulz (same-shape matrices across leaves in one batched call) | equal within bf16 rounding; optimizer cost now ~noise | → 650.6 (+8%) |
| CE vocab tile 4096 → 8192 | step-0 loss identical; trajectory in replicate spread | ~638 → 658 (+3%) |
| sort-based MoE receiver ranks; gather-based MoE expand backward; KDA chunk states saved at d512 | exact-output tests (bitwise-identical grads for KDA) | compute 169.8 → 160.5 ms/step |
| one GEMM for each MoE block's input projections (router, latent down, shared gate/up) + one for shared down-projections | CPU grad parity < 1e-5 rel | 648 → 692 |
| **final default build** | 400-step loss inside the original-vs-original envelope; step-0 loss matches to 1e-5 | **469.6 → 691.2 (+47%)**, MFU 6.72 → 9.89, peak 31.9 GiB |
| opt-in: f32 embedding-grad accumulation (`--model-set embed_grad_accumulation=float32`; changes rounding) | full B run 3.1010 (no loss cost) | 691 → 738 (+6.8%) |
| opt-in: XLA command buffers (`--xla_gpu_enable_command_buffer=FUSION`; off due to #5675 B200 hang) | full run completed | +1.5% |
| both opt-ins | | 749.8 (+60%), MFU 10.73 |
Tried, no gain, reverted: PGLE, exact argmax top-k, saved MoE expert activations, fused KDA q/k/v/gate projections, disabling the inline watch. Remaining ~185 ms/step: ~155 compute + ~19 exposed comm (MoE dispatch/combine/a2a/experts ~49 + a2a, KDA ~32, CE ~12, MLA ~13.5, router top_k 6.7, AttnRes mix ~6.7).

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **MLA K-ShortConv and inference absorbability (KMA, original ladder recipe; single seeds)**

The fast_track baseline applies a depthwise causal ShortConv (kernel 4) to k **after** the MLA W_UK up-projection (`CausalSelfAttention.sconv_k`, `sconv_sites` "k"). That breaks single-matrix W_UK absorption at inference. KDA's own q/k/v convs (`kda_sconv_sites`) are unaffected. Options tested (branch `fast-track-kma-kconv`): **no K conv** (`--model-set sconv_sites=attn,mlp`); **A** latent conv on the K path only, `k = W_UK·conv(c)`, `v = W_UV·c` (absorbable; cache conv(c) too, or 4 taps on the absorbed query); **B** shared latent conv `c' = conv(c)` feeding K and V (zero inference overhead: cache c', standard absorption); **C** conv before the down-projection `c = W_DKV·conv(x)`.

| size | with K conv (ref) | no K conv | A (latent, K only) | B (shared latent) | C (before W_DKV) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| d512 | 3.1138 (5-seed mean) | 3.1341 (**+0.020**) | 3.1137 (0.000) | 3.1204 (+0.007) | 3.1209 (+0.007) |
| d768 | [kma-d768](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/kma-d768) 2.8193 | [kc-d768-nok](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/kc-d768-nok) 2.8242 (**+0.005**) | [kc-d768-lk](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/kc-d768-lk) 2.8185 (−0.001) | [kc-d768-ls](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/kc-d768-ls) 2.8214 (+0.002) | – |
| d1024 | [kma-d1024](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/kma-d1024) 2.5852 | kc-d1024-nok (running) | – | – | – |

All options are free in training throughput. The cost of dropping the conv shrinks 4× from d512 to d768; A fully recovers it at both sizes; B (zero inference overhead) is within noise at d768 → likely the practical choice at scale.

Also: KMA d1024 final **2.5852** (−0.048 vs 2.6330, ≈1.50× compute; old build at 0.795× throughput → ≈1.19× effective, before the identical-math speedups).

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Update: init/optimizer studies, final-gate MLPs, wide KDA, K-conv at d1024, KDA d1280.** All results are on the B0 KMA recipe, one seed each unless stated otherwise. Metric is final Paloma macro loss. B0 d512 = 3.1112 (5-seed mean, σ≈0.002); B0 d768 = 2.8096.

### MuonH init and Muon vs MuonH per group (branch `fast-track-muonh-init`)
- **Init scale is a no-op under MuonH.** MuonH holds each matrix at its init Frobenius norm, so an init multiplier just becomes a fixed output scale on that matrix. A following RMSNorm or `qk_mult` cancels it, or Adam-trained gains downstream absorb it. Every init sweep was within noise (3.109–3.122).
- **Plain Muon (no hyperball) loses almost everywhere.**
  - All groups on Muon, no weight decay: 3.1519.
  - Routed experts: 3.1472. KDA: 3.1199. MLA: 3.1150.
  - Without weight decay, norms drift up 2.5–4×, which shrinks the effective step.
- **Where it wins:** GatedNorms on plain Muon with weight decay, and the LatentMoE latent at a lower LR.

| Config (on top of B0) | d512 | d768 |
|---|---|---|
| B0 | 3.1112 | 2.8096 |
| GatedNorms on Muon wd 0.05 + latent on MuonH at LR ×0.5 | **3.1019** | 2.8074 |
| GatedNorms + shared + latent on Muon wd 0.05 | 3.1038 | **2.8064** |
| Latent on MuonH at LR ×0.5 only | 3.1057 | – |
| GatedNorms only, Muon wd 0.05 | 3.1059 | – |

- **Weight decay:** 0.03–0.1 is the useful range; 0.2 loses the gain. wd 0.05 and 0.1 give equal loss despite different norm paths, so the gain comes from the effective step size changing over training, not from a target norm.
- **Scale:** the gain is −0.009 at d512 but only −0.002 to −0.003 at d768 (about 1.02× compute), which is marginal.
- **Per-group LR schedules are all noise (3.1076–3.1101).** The groups tested were the KDA gate, `A_log`/`dt_bias` and β, the MLA latent norms, the AttnRes queries and Inkling. The schedules tried were no decay, WSD (hold then decay over the last 30%), an LR floor and a longer warmup. The one exception is a 10% warmup on the AttnRes queries, which hurts (3.1205).

### μP steelman (branch `fast-track-mup`)
μP never beats B0.
- **Why:** MuonH/AdamH are already spectral-μP for hidden matrices, so μP reduces to per-class init plus a width-constant LR. B0's fitted LR decay with width (d^-0.345) transfers better.
- **d512:** μP is identical to B0 by construction. Its LR and multiplier sweep is centred at ×1 (fitted LR optimum ×1.05).
- **d768:**
  - textbook μP 2.8150 (+0.005);
  - μP with lm_head kept at 1/√d: 2.8116 (+0.002);
  - B0 LRs plus μP input-class init: 2.8089 (tie).
- **d1024:** B0 2.5860 vs μP (lm_head at 1/√d) 2.5930 (+0.007). The gap grows with width.
- **Coordinate check:** the 1/d output rule shrinks logits, router logits and GatedNorm logits with width at these sizes.

### AttnRes final gate as an MLP (d512, 2 seeds each)
None beats B0's single learned final query. Every variant is 1–4% slower.

| Final gate | Mean | Δ |
|---|---|---|
| Joint MLP over all blocks, zero bias | 3.1103 | 0.000 |
| Key MLP (d→64→1 per block) | 3.1118 | +0.0015 |
| Logits MLP | 3.1133 | +0.003 |
| Joint, bias init favoring early / late blocks | 3.1184 / 3.1172 | +0.008 / +0.007 |
| Query MLP (1 seed) | 3.1203 | +0.010 |

- At 0.1× Adam LR the biases barely move: ±0.03 from zero init, and the ±1 ramps end where they started.
- The fix for a GPU garbage-gradient bug with an MLP final gate (`da5c519378`) also makes every AttnRes run slightly cheaper.

### Other single changes on B0
- **1.5× KDA heads:**
  - d512 3.1040 (−0.007), d768 2.8050 (−0.0046).
  - Throughput is 7–10% lower, so the net effective speedup is about 0.93–0.97×. Not adopted.
- **No XSA:** 3.1302 (+0.019, worse).
- **Neutral:** per-channel attention gate 3.1131; MoE latent RMSNorm init 2 3.1113.

### MLA K-conv removal vs scale

| Size | Loss without K-conv (Δ) |
|---|---|
| d512 | +0.020 |
| d768 | +0.005 |
| d1024 | +0.0037 (2.5891 vs 2.5854) |

A conv on the latent's K path only keeps MLA absorbable and fully recovers the loss at d512 and d768.

### Ladder
- KDA COMBO d1280: **2.4813, −0.022 vs baseline** (d512–d1024: −0.019 / −0.032 / −0.023).
- MLA+AttnRes d1280 and KMA d1280 are still running.

The September 28 tier-3 ferry failed in `verify_fuzzy_dups`: only 285 of its 1,000 requested workers became ready, and `load_memory_store` raised `TimeoutError` after the 1,800-second readiness wait. `consolidate` and `tokenize` did not run. This is the fourth consecutive weekly failure with the signature tracked in #8948.

Reproduce:
1. Run the scheduled datakit-nemotron tier-3 ferry with `FERRY_TEST_MAX_FILES=1000` in `europe-west4`.
2. At `verify_fuzzy_dups`, observe the 1,000-worker pool (`cpu=16`, `ram=160g` per worker) and the wait for all workers in `lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/context.py:402`.
3. When fewer than 1,000 workers are ready after 1,800 seconds, the driver raises `TimeoutError` and fails the step.

Expected: verification can complete when the full 1,000-worker pool cannot become ready within the timeout.

Evidence: the verify coordinator's durable Iris log last recorded `285/1000 ready` at 07:04:01 UTC. The driver raised `TimeoutError` at 07:27:44 UTC; the [Actions wait step](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/36384287011/job/108806301093) reported `RuntimeError: 1 step(s) failed`. The [uploaded diagnostics artifact](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/36384287011/artifacts/10955759016) contains the job tree. Its child jobs' `Terminated by user` reason came from teardown when the driver timed out.

## Overview

What is this document? This document is an attempt to formalize Marin’s policy towards what constitutes reportable, public-facing, canonical eval results for Marin models as well as the baselines we compare against.

Why do we need this document? With the first “snowball” release of a 67B A2B MoE, Marin is entering a regime where we regularly compare Marin models to existing open and closed-source models. Because Marin’s unique claim is that we are open development, we will need to hold ourselves to a high standard of transparency on how we report eval scores of Marin models and what claims we make about Marin model capabilities based on those scores.

What is in scope for this document? This document is intended to act as a living snapshot, trustworthy for any given period in time, as to the what and the how of Marin’s canonical set of evals, a set of standards to which we will aspire to hold ourselves. By "the what", we mean “which evals did we run, with what consistent set of hyperparameters and experimental constraints”. By "the how", we mean “where is the self-contained codebase that is both necessary and sufficient to reproduce our eval results independently”.

## Previous version notes

* Released Sept 16, 2026: 11 Evalchemy benchmarks, 8 lm-eval-harness tasks and 5 Harbor agentic evals in-distribution

- **MATH-500.** OpenAI's [May 2023 process-supervision release](https://openai.com/index/improving-mathematical-reasoning-with-process-supervision/) used a 500-problem subset of the original MATH competition-math benchmark. The campaign scores one zero-shot generated solution per problem by final-answer accuracy.
- **HumanEval+.** The [May 2023 EvalPlus paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.01210) introduced expanded tests for HumanEval programs to catch incorrect code that passes sparse original tests. The campaign executes one zero-shot completion per problem against the stronger tests.
- **MBPP+.** The [November 24, 2023 EvalPlus release](https://github.com/evalplus/evalplus/releases/tag/v0.2.0) extends MBPP with additional functional tests. The campaign's pinned config is zero-shot and scores one generated program per problem.
- **OlympiadBench.** The [February 2024 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.14008) introduced bilingual, multimodal Olympiad-level math and science problems. This campaign uses Evalchemy's 30-question text subset, ten sampled solutions per question, and the configured answer judge.
- **GSM8K.** The [October 2021 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.14168) introduced grade-school math word problems requiring multi-step arithmetic. The campaign uses the zero-shot `gsm8k-0shot` completion route and scores the extracted final answer.
- **PIQA.** The [November 2019 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.11641) introduced two-choice questions about physical commonsense. The campaign selects the answer by length-normalized log-likelihood with no examples in the prompt.
- **WinoGrande.** The [July 2019 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.10641) introduced adversarial pronoun/coreference choices designed to reduce superficial cues. The campaign uses five-shot multiple-choice scoring.
- **BoolQ.** The [May 2019 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.10044) introduced naturally occurring yes/no questions paired with evidence passages. The campaign scores zero-shot choice accuracy.
- **TruthfulQA MC2.** The [September 2021 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.07958) introduced questions that elicit common misconceptions from language models. The campaign's MC2 metric sums probability mass on all true answers within each question's candidate set, rather than counting a single selected answer.
- **TriviaQA.** The [May 2017 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.03551) introduced trivia questions with independently collected evidence documents. The campaign runs five-shot answer generation and reports answer accuracy.
- **AIME24.** The [Mathematical Association of America's 2024 AIME](https://maa.org/maa-invitational-competitions/) supplies the contest problems; AIME24 is a year-specific evaluation set, not a separately introduced research benchmark. Evalchemy samples ten solutions per question through the benchmark's built-in repeat loop and scores the integer final answers. The campaign ran that 30-question, ten-repeat protocol ten times, for 3,000 generations per model. The preserved launch records have `evalchemy.seed: null`, so the outer launches were not ten distinct random seeds; every launch used the same benchmark-internal repeat seed schedule.
- **MMLU-Pro.** The [June 2024 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.01574) introduced harder, more reasoning-focused multiple-choice questions across fourteen subjects. The campaign runs zero-shot generation with a 65,536-token cap and reports micro-averaged accuracy.
- **GPQA Diamond.** The [November 2023 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.12022) introduced expert-written graduate-level science questions, including the Diamond subset. The campaign averages accuracy over three generated answers per question.
- **CRUXEval (output).** The [January 2024 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.03065) introduced input- and output-prediction tasks for short Python programs. The tracker reports the output-prediction direction, scored on one generated answer per item.
- **FinanceBench.** The [November 2023 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.11944) introduced questions grounded in public financial filings. The campaign scores one generated answer per question with its pinned LLM judge.
- **IFBench.** The [July 2025 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.02833) introduced verifiable constraints that test generalization in precise instruction following. The campaign reports strict prompt-level accuracy, requiring every constraint to hold in the raw response.
- **MRCR.** [Gemini's September 2024 report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.12640) introduced multi-round coreference resolution; [OpenAI's public MRCR release (April 2025)](https://huggingface.co/datasets/openai/mrcr) supplies the corrected multi-needle data used here. The campaign scores nonce-gated sequence similarity and selects only context-length bins that fit the served model.
- **NUPA.** The [November 2024 Number Cookbook paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.03766) introduced tests of numerical understanding and processing across representations and tasks. Existing tracker scores use the full Evalchemy protocol of 238,926 selected prompts.
- **SWE-bench Verified random-100.** OpenAI's [August 13, 2024 release](https://openai.com/index/introducing-swe-bench-verified/) introduced a human-validated subset of repository-issue repair tasks. The campaign evaluates a fixed random 100-task subset of this existing subset, with one Terminus-2 trial per issue and executable verification.
- **OpenThoughts-TBLite 2.0.** The [February 18, 2026 release](https://www.openthoughts.ai/blog/openthoughts-tblite) introduced a 100-task, faster-running terminal-agent panel calibrated against Terminal-Bench 2. The campaign runs its pinned `openthoughts-tblite@2.0` tasks with Terminus-2 and reports verifier success.
- **Terminal-Bench 2.0.** The [November 7, 2025 release](https://www.tbench.ai/news/announcement-2-0) introduced a harder, more thoroughly verified terminal-agent task set alongside Harbor. The campaign uses the pinned TB2 dataset through Harbor with one Terminus-2 trial per task.
- **DS-1000 mini-200.** The [November 2022 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.11501) introduced data-science code-generation problems spanning seven Python libraries. The campaign evaluates a fixed seed-42 200-task Harbor subset with Terminus-2, building task images from the pinned Dockerfiles.
- **BFCL-Parity @ Pi.** Berkeley's [February 2024 BFCL release](https://gorilla.cs.berkeley.edu/blogs/8_berkeley_function_calling_leaderboard.html) introduced executable function-calling evaluation. This campaign uses the Harbor `bfcl_parity@1.0` adaptation with the Pi agent, so its score is the pinned adaptation's verified solve rate rather than an unqualified BFCL leaderboard score.
- **BixBench CLI corrections @ Pi.** The [February 2025 BixBench paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.00096) introduced multi-step computational-biology analysis tasks. This campaign uses Pi on 205 `bixbench-cli-marin-corrections@3` tasks and reports binary answer-equivalence reward, which is distinct from canonical BixBench CLI v1.5.
- **τ³-bench @ Pi.** Sierra's [March 18, 2026 τ³-Bench launch](https://sierra.ai/blog/bench-advancing-agent-benchmarking-to-knowledge-and-voice) introduced knowledge and voice tracks alongside corrections to the existing airline and retail tasks. The campaign runs pinned `tau3-bench@1.0.1` in Harbor through the Pi ACP relay and scores task verification.
- **SOTOPIA-hard.** The [October 2023 SOTOPIA paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.11667) introduced interactive social-agent evaluation and identified a hard scenario subset. The campaign runs the 100 hard episodes against a fixed `openai/gpt-oss-120b` counterpart and judge, then normalizes goal achievement from 0–10 to 0–1.

### How do we handle in-distribution and out-of-distribution evals?

#### IN-DISTRIBUTION

**We will** -- dedup against our SFT data, look at model scores while we develop the model, inspect the correlation of our ID evals with our OOD evals

**We may** -- develop synthetic RL tasks modeled on specific tasks in ID evals

**We will not** -- train on teacher rollouts from eval questions, use our ID eval instructions directly as the basis of RL data

#### OUT-OF-DISTRIBUTION

**We will** -- de-dup against our SFT raw data, look at meta-data about these evals (e.g., how big they are, general knowledge domain, etc), eval baselines on these evals

**We may** -- evaluate our final models on out-of-distribution benchmarks

**We will not** -- look at the individual questions in the evals, look at any of our own model scores from these evals until our model is frozen, model any synthetic tasks on tasks in the evals (edited)

### Metric definitions

- **`accuracy`:** the fraction of scored items that pass the benchmark's configured correctness check. The common name covers executable-test success for code and agent tasks, answer correctness for generated and multiple-choice tasks, FinanceBench's `correct` judge label, and BixBench's binary answer-equivalence check. NUPA counts an item as correct only when its format-specific extraction produces a representation-sensitive exact match. PIQA chooses the option with the highest length-normalized log-likelihood before testing correctness. AIME24 first averages its ten built-in repeats per question and then averages across ten outer launches; the outer launches did not pass distinct seeds. GPQA-Diamond and OlympiadBench average their three and ten in-run repeats per question. MMLU-Pro is micro-averaged across its fourteen subjects.
- **`mc2`:** TruthfulQA's probability mass on all true answers, normalized over the question's answer set and averaged over questions. It is not a binary selection accuracy, and chance performance is above zero.
- **`accuracy (output)`:** CRUXEval output-prediction accuracy. Given a function and input, the model predicts the output; this is distinct from CRUXEval input prediction, which reconstructs an input from the function and desired output.
- **`strict prompt-level accuracy`:** the fraction of IFBench prompts for which the raw response satisfies every required constraint.
- **`mean sequence similarity`:** MRCR's mean `SequenceMatcher` ratio between the response's answer span and the reference answer. A response that fails MRCR's nonce check receives zero credit. The standard 73,728-token serving window evaluates the published bins through 65,536 tokens. After Marin's 64-token serving safety margin, the 32,768-token models use bins through 16,384 and the 65,536-token model uses bins through 32,768. Those tracker cells are footnoted because differing bin coverage is not a strictly like-for-like comparison.
- **`normalized goal achievement`:** SOTOPIA-hard's official goal-achievement score for the evaluated character, linearly normalized from `[0, 10]` to `[0, 1]` and averaged over the 100 official hard episodes. The counterpart and evaluator are fixed to `openai/gpt-oss-120b` on Together for every model.

### Other Metric Notes

- **Scale:** every metric in the suite is reported on a 0-1 scale with 1 the best and 0 the worst; there are no error counts, ranks, or unbounded scores.
- **Allowed context length:** This is allowed prompt + completion context length. If a model's maximum context length is less than the allowed context length, we adopt the model's maximum context length. For single-turn benchmarks, we subdivide the space into max prompt length = longest prompt in the dataset plus a bit of cushion, max response length = the remaining context window. For standard multi-turn benchmarks, max generation length per turn is capped at 8192. Context-ablation labels are `context window / per-turn output limit`: both values are passed explicitly, with the first applied to vLLM `max_model_len` and Pi `model_info.max_input_tokens`, and the second applied to Pi `model_info.max_output_tokens`. For example, `65k-16k` means a 65,536-token serving and Pi context window with a 16,384-token per-turn output limit.
- **Pi runtime:** Agentic Pi configs must pin `@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent` explicitly. The corrected context control pins Pi `0.87.0`; the original harness result used unpinned Pi `0.86.1`, while the first context-ablation rerun drifted to unpinned Pi `0.87.0`. Results from different Pi versions are not treated as a controlled context-only comparison.

### LLM judges

Four evals involve an LLM judge; every other eval in the suite grades programmatically
(IFBench verifies each constraint with its checker functions, MRCR uses `SequenceMatcher`,
the math evals use Minerva/SymPy, the multiple-choice evals compare selections, and the
harness/agentic evals run test suites).

- **FinanceBench:** every scored response is judged. The judge sees the question, the
  reference answers, and the candidate, and returns one label: `correct`, `incorrect`, or
  `not_attempted` (equivalent answers in substance count as correct — algebraic equivalence,
  unit conversions, rounding). Only `correct` scores.
- **BixBench CLI correction set:** every submitted answer is judged for semantic equivalence
  to the task's ideal answer and receives a binary reward. A missing answer receives zero
  without invoking the judge.
- **OlympiadBench:** Minerva/SymPy grades first, and the judge answers equivalence only for
  answers Minerva cannot establish; the reported scores come from the offline regrade, which
  uses this judge the same way (see "OlympiadBench regrade" below).
- **SOTOPIA-hard:** the official episode evaluator judges goal achievement for the evaluated
  character after each completed social interaction and returns the 0–10 score that the metric
  normalizes to 0–1.

The standard judge for all four is `openai/gpt-oss-120b` served through Together
(`JUDGE_MODEL`/`JUDGE_BASE_URL` in the launch commands; the credential is the Together API
key). Open weights and one model everywhere keep judge behavior consistent across evals and
runs, and reproducible anywhere Together (or a self-serve vLLM deployment of the same
checkpoint) is available. τ³'s LiteLLM client uses `openai/openai/gpt-oss-120b`: the first
segment selects LiteLLM's OpenAI-compatible provider and the remainder is Together's model ID.
Judge hyperparameters, per path:

- **Answer-equivalence judge** (FinanceBench, OlympiadBench): a single user message with the
  three-way rubric, `temperature=0`, request timeout 300 s with 5 transport retries, and 16
  concurrent judgments per run. `max_tokens` starts at 128 and escalates 128 → 512 → 2048
  when a completion comes back empty — a hosted reasoning model can spend a small completion
  budget on hidden reasoning and return no content — so the ladder guarantees the final label
  lands within budget. The context window is gpt-oss-120b's 131,072 tokens as served
  (Together); no truncation of the graded material happens judge-side. The raw completion is
  retained in the results for audit, alongside the parsed label.
- **BixBench verifier:** the verifier calls Chat Completions with `max_tokens=1024` and a
  structured response schema containing one boolean score. Sampling follows the endpoint's
  service defaults.
- **SOTOPIA evaluator:** the pinned SOTOPIA v0.1.5 evaluator uses the fixed judge model after
  each episode; the model under evaluation never acts as its own judge.

When a judge call fails after retries, the sample is recorded as grader infrastructure
failure (counted against the run's error tolerance) rather than silently scored zero.

### Thinking mode

The main table records the policy for every benchmark. `on` and `off` set
`enable_thinking` through the model or benchmark config; a benchmark override wins over the model
default. `model default` means the benchmark adds no override, and `not applicable` means the task

### Errors and Exceptions

#### Infrastructure Error Tolerance

Modern benchmarks are prone to encountering transient infrastructure errors. Our policy is to allow a degree of tolerance for infrastructure error; up to 10% of a benchmark's tasks can be invalidated by an infrastructure failure before we invalidate the entire score for a model on the benchmark. We do not attempt to control for the particular infrastructure errors that were encountered by various models on particular tasks. For this reason, we report confidence intervals as slightly wider than they would be if all models had reported on all tasks.

#### Infrastructure vs Model Error

We categorize errors during the evaluation process as either infrastructure errors or model errors.
Model errors are scoreable and do not count toward the infrastructure-error threshold. Unless this
policy explicitly identifies an error as a model error, it is an infrastructure error.

For Harbor evals, the following error types are currently treated as score-able model errors.

- `AgentTimeoutError`: the agent reached its configured execution timeout; Harbor preserves
  the work produced so far and runs the verifier.
- `ContextLengthExceededError`: the model or agent exhausted the available context; Harbor
  treats that as a classified end to the attempt and runs the verifier.
- `TurnCapExhaustedError`: the agent reached its configured turn cap without declaring
  completion; Harbor runs the verifier on the resulting state.
- `NonZeroAgentExitCodeError`: the agent process exited non-zero after potentially producing
  scoreable work; Harbor still runs the verifier. Agent-specific subclasses must be reported
  under their concrete exception type and reviewed for validity rather than silently grouped.

For these Harbor score-able model errors, we terminate the trial and then run the verifier on the output of the agent, if any output is present. Unlike the Evalchemy timeout rule above, we do *not* automatically score Harbor model errors as 0's. This is because sometimes, agents will solve the task correctly and then get stuck in a loop of self-doubt or fail to submit properly in their harness, and we regard that outcome as closer to a success than a failure.

#### Timeout Policy

The following limits apply to every policy benchmark; there are no benchmark-specific exceptions.

| Evaluator phase | Limit | Outcome when the limit expires |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Evalchemy trial | 30 minutes | Record `0.0` as an `AgentTimeoutError`. This is a scoreable model outcome. |
| Harbor agent setup | 6 minutes | Record `AgentSetupTimeoutError`. This is a retryable infrastructure error. |
| Harbor agent execution | 30 minutes | Record `AgentTimeoutError`, preserve the agent's work, and run the verifier. This is a scoreable model outcome. |
| Harbor verifier | 5 minutes | Record `VerifierTimeoutError`. This is a retryable infrastructure error. |

The Evalchemy limit covers the full trial, including request retries and backoff, after the trial
acquires an evaluator slot. Evalchemy [#175](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/pull/175)
implements the deadline, and campaign configs set `timeout=1800`.

Harbor launch configs override task-manifest values with
`agents[].override_setup_timeout_sec: 360`, `agents[].override_timeout_sec: 1800`, and
`verifier.override_timeout_sec: 300`. `artifacts/common.sh` checks these values before submission,
so the same limits apply even when a task manifest omits its own timeout.

## Baseline Models

### How we select baseline models

The process for selecting baseline models in our policy is fundamentally heuristic and community-driven. For each new model release, we will strive to select a representative cohort of open-weights and open-source models that are roughly comparable to Marin models and document them in the policy. We will look up reported results for those models in the research literature and, where available, use them as targets for internal reproduction, noting, however, that typically the variance in hyperparameters will make published results not directly comparable to our own. We will sometimes substitute quantized variants of the listed models for the canonical models, especially for larger models where our hardware makes it challenging to run inference on the non-quantized variants.

Run the Harbor evaluations from a separate directory so Harbor's environment does not share
Evalchemy's project environment:

```bash

cd harbor

uv sync --all-packages

export MODEL_BASE_URL=https://example-model-endpoint.invalid/v1
export MODEL_ID="REPLACE_WITH_SERVED_MODEL_NAME"
export MODEL_API_KEY="REPLACE_WITH_MODEL_ENDPOINT_API_KEY"
export TOGETHER_API_KEY="REPLACE_WITH_TOGETHER_API_KEY"
export DAYTONA_API_KEY="REPLACE_WITH_DAYTONA_API_KEY"
export OPENAI_API_KEY="$TOGETHER_API_KEY"

export TAU2_NL_ASSERTIONS_MODEL="$TAU2_USER_MODEL"

for config in swebench-recovery ot-tblite-recovery tb2-recovery ds-1000-local \
              bfclparity-pi bixbench-pi tau3-pi; do
  uv run harbor run \
    --config "$ARTIFACTS/harbor-configs/$config.yaml" \
    --model "hosted_vllm/$MODEL_ID" \
    --ak "api_base=${MODEL_BASE_URL%/}" \
    --ak 'model_info={"max_input_tokens":32768,"max_output_tokens":8192,"input_cost_per_token":0.0,"output_cost_per_token":0.0}' \
    --ae "OPENAI_API_KEY=$MODEL_API_KEY" \
    --jobs-dir "results/harbor/$config" --yes
done

# From the Harbor root, this writes datasets/sotopia-hard, the path used by the saved config.

  --config "$ARTIFACTS/harbor-configs/sotopia-hard-standalone.yaml" \
  --model "hosted_vllm/$MODEL_ID" \
  --ak "api_base=${MODEL_BASE_URL%/}" \
  --ae "OPENAI_API_KEY=$MODEL_API_KEY" \
  --jobs-dir results/harbor/sotopia-hard --yes
```

## Run resumption

Resume an interrupted Harbor run only when its model, evaluator pins, runtime limit, and dataset
state are unchanged. Find the Iris root in `artifacts/config-snapshots/launches.jsonl`, then use
that snapshot's `launch.json` and copied YAML files. Replay its saved arguments with only the
affected Harbor config, retaining any `--limit` and `--records-prefix`, and add the original run ID:

```bash
uv run python -m experiments.evaluation.cli launch \
  --model-config artifacts/config-snapshots/launches/<snapshot-id>/<model-config>.yaml \
  --harbor-config artifacts/config-snapshots/launches/<snapshot-id>/<harbor-config>.yaml \
  --resume-run-id <original-run-id>
```

The durable `<records-prefix>/<original-run-id>/results/harbor_jobs/` tree must remain accessible.
Harbor preserves completed scored trials and reruns missing attempts and exceptions in its pinned
resume taxonomy. Use a clean replacement when model, policy, pins, limits, records prefix, or
dataset state changed, or when the unscored error is outside that taxonomy. Never delete a trial
directory to force recovery.

## Baseline-specific launch settings

The YAML files under `artifacts/model-configs/` are authoritative for checkpoint and tokenizer
revisions, serving context, GPU count, tensor and data parallelism, reasoning parser, tool parser,
sampling overrides, and Pi `thinking_format`. Use the matching file unchanged. Pi uses
`qwen-chat-template` for Qwen3.6 and Qwen3-Next and `chat-template` for the other models.

MRCR serves at 73,728 tokens and gives Evalchemy 73,664 after its 64-token safety margin. Ling
Lite's native 32,768-token window uses `mrcr-32k.yaml`; the historical 65,536-token Snowball
candidate uses `mrcr-65k.yaml`; every release-figure model uses `mrcr.yaml` otherwise. Evalchemy
evaluates only the published bins that fit.

K2 Horizon adds `--chat-template-content-format string` to vLLM. Its OlympiadBench, TriviaQA,
MMLU-Pro, and GPQA-Diamond runs use eight H100s, tensor parallelism 2, data parallelism 4, a 512 GiB
serve-worker memory request, and 16 concurrent Evalchemy requests. The serve settings are in
`artifacts/model-configs/IFM-K2-Horizon-MoVA-36B-A4B.yaml`; the evaluator command sets concurrency,
and the immutable launch snapshots preserve both.

## Updating codebase pins

Use the newest campaign pin for each codebase across the full release, assuming forward
compatibility with earlier score-producing runs. If a pin change causes an observed result
regression, stop launches, fix or revert the change, and issue a new policy version when the
evaluation behavior intentionally changes. Preserve the original run's exact pins in its immutable
config snapshot even after the release-wide pins advance.

## Standards for presenting Marin evals

* Select the release Snowball checkpoint by simple paired benchmark win rate among Snowball candidates. Release figures include only the selected checkpoint, not the other Snowball candidates. The Snowball candidate family includes the Grug 67B A2B checkpoint as well as checkpoints named Snowball. For each benchmark, plot the selected Snowball checkpoint and every non-Snowball baseline with an available score and total-training-FLOP estimate. Performance is on the y-axis and total training FLOPs are on a logarithmic x-axis. A baseline with an incomplete suite may appear in the scatterplots for its completed benchmarks, but it is excluded from cross-benchmark critical-difference analysis unless it has the full common benchmark panel.
* Produce uncertainty-aware normalized critical-difference diagrams with and without a FLOP control. Normalize scores within each benchmark across the complete-panel cohort. Estimate each score's task-level sample SEM from the scored trial rewards, then multiply the SEM by `1 / sqrt(0.9)` to account conservatively for the policy's 10% infrastructure-failure tolerance. With a fixed random seed, draw 100,000 score panels from independent normal sampling distributions centered on the reported scores and clipped to the metric's `[0, 1]` range. Rank models within every benchmark for each draw, using average ranks for ties, and report mean ranks with simultaneous 95% bands based on the draw-wise maximum absolute rank deviation. Report the Nemenyi critical difference at `alpha = 0.05`; it depends on the number of models and benchmarks, while score uncertainty affects the simulated rank distribution and its simultaneous bands.
* For the FLOP-controlled diagram, regress the draw's benchmark-normalized scores on `log10(total training FLOPs)` with one common linear slope, rank the within-benchmark residuals, and otherwise use the same uncertainty procedure. Treat FLOP estimates as fixed point estimates and disclose that their estimation uncertainty is not propagated. The uncontrolled diagram ranks the sampled normalized scores directly.
* We use a 6ND proxy for pretraining FLOPS, and 6 * max_tokens_per_rollout / max_context_length * n_rollouts * active_params proxy for RL FLOPS; that said, we are the only lab, as of this writing, which releases RL FLOPS, so meaningful comparisons are impossible. From the few labs who release midtraining / SFT information, we derive an unweighted mean percentage of FLOPS devoted to midtraining. We then estimate midtraining FLOPS for other labs using that mean. We estimate total FLOPS as the sum of pretraining FLOPS + (all midtraining / non-RL) FLOPS + (all RL and OPD) FLOPS. For any model which doesn't give sufficient evidence for any of the three stages, use the mean FLOPS over all models in the cohort as the estimated  FLOPS for that stage.
* In a separate standalone table, include all raw scores in XX.y format, with 95% confidence intervals derived from the trial count and the infrastructure error tolerance -- do not leave gaps, use table captions for results that require further context, use the exact same model family in the table as was present in the x-y scatterplot(s)
* Eval results are reportable IFF the eval in question completed with <10% of trials encountering infrastructure errors
* Eval results are reportable IFF they include provenance, in the form of model traces, and where available, verifier traces
* Any eval result that is publicly presented should clearly distinguish whether the benchmarks are in-distribution (part of the dev set), held out, or a mix of the two
* Any eval result that is publicly presented in a major release should report on *all* ID and OOD benchmarks, avoiding cherry picking, substitution, or new evals outside of a formal policy update
* For active development and internal communication, it is fine to define working subsets of the ID benchmarks and report on those in isolation

## Future considerations

* We would like to post-train multiple Snowball checkpoints, experimenting with different degrees of compute applied to post-training, to establish trade-off lines / domains
* We would like to think about a "marin model card" that would set minimum standards for true open development
* amd/Instella-MoE-16B-A3B-Think is not runnable currently from our pinned vLLM fork, but we would like to look at this model in the future

issues.author: weaverbot
issues.body:
The weekly fork-migration system from #8048 is in place: a refresh-fork skill and
per-fork descriptors (#8068, #8117), a weekly ferry coordinator (#8245) with Loom
federation (#8284), and automated re-pinning for the vLLM GPU wheel (#8292). The TPU
vLLM stack refreshed to tpu-inference v0.26.0 (#8207) on top of the externalized
stack (#8063), and the GPU wheel now discovers its `_C` extension by shape across the
CUDA 13 / stable-ABI boundary (#8250). This issue tracks the work that remains after
that rollout, and is the canonical fork-migration tracker going forward. It supersedes
#8048 and folds in the refresh trackers #8298, #7097, #7143, and #6480.

1. Promote the Harbor one-time catch-up. marin-community/harbor#73 re-ports the fork
   overlay onto current upstream and folds the standalone `harbor-config` package into
   `harbor.models`. It is mergeable with `marin-precommit`, `marin-style-sync`, and
   `tests` green. Two steps need an admin/reviewer: drop the retired `harbor-config`
   context from the fork `main` branch protection (it no longer reports, so it blocks
   the merge), then review and merge, and promote the caught-up tree to protected
   `main`. Done when fork `main` carries the caught-up overlay and its protection no
   longer requires `harbor-config`.

2. Bump the Marin Harbor pin. After harbor#73 lands, re-pin `config/external/harbor`
   to the landed `main` SHA, migrate the `harbor_config.*` imports in
   `lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/trial_driver.py` to `harbor.models.*`, and
   keep the migration.toml [harbor] nuances. The aime-smoke e2e already passed
   end-to-end against the catch-up branch on qwen3-0.6b. Closes out the blocker path
   #8298.

3. Migrate MarinSkyRL as a managed Harbor consumer (#7920). The SkyRL fork depends on
   `harbor[analysis,datasets,daytona]` floating on `main` plus the standalone
   `harbor-config` wheel, so the harbor.models fold in harbor#73 breaks any SkyRL
   relock. Pin harbor to an explicit immutable ref, migrate off `harbor-config` to
   `harbor.models`, and give SkyRL a Marin-style update-external plus one terminal-bench
   e2e. Cadence stays decoupled and coordinated on breaking changes rather than weekly
   lockstep. Tracked under #7920.

4. Make the ferry's evalchemy leg observable. The weekly run produced no PR and filed
   no blocker for evalchemy. Confirm whether that is a legitimate no-op (the fork
   already matches upstream `main`) or a silent failure, and have the leg emit an
   explicit no-op summary either way.

5. Publish prebuilt TPU vLLM fork wheels (#7143). Cold TPU jobs still source-build the
   `vllm` and `tpu-inference` forks; a Marin-controlled index would let serve, eval,
   and RL install a pinned wheel. Standalone spec in #7143.

6. Resolve the Marin-owned pin audit (#6480). Decide whether Levanter can move to a
   Transformers 5 range and drop the tpu-inference Gemma4 guard, and keep the
   JAX/libtpu/torch/torchvision alignment documented against the fork stack. The
   descriptor records these as nuances; the decision is open. Spec in #6480.

issues.body:
The `vllm-gpu` refresh cannot publish or qualify a wheel from `main-next` before the protected `main` hard swap. The [candidate workflow](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/blob/01911be34fac8715347962a8d791ca34a879e01e/.github/workflows/marin-gpu-candidate.yaml) calls `verify-main-lineage` before GPU publication. issues.author: rjpower
issues.body:
`ReadView.point` reads every shard of its table, so one keyed lookup costs time proportional to the number of shards. `_read_plan` calls `pq.read_schema` on each shard, and `_scan_plan` then scans each shard with the key filter. The manifest's `Shard` records no key range, so no shard can be skipped. `open_blob` pays this twice: once in the `blobs` descriptor table and once in `_finestore_blob_parts`. Blobs small enough to store inline sit in `blobs` itself, so the descriptor scan also downloads their data.

With one transaction per blob, lookup time grows linearly with the number of blobs written. On local disk, `resolve` of a single blob took 0.019 s with 25 descriptor shards, 0.067 s with 100, and 0.309 s with 400. On S3 each shard adds round trips. In a MarinSkyRL async RL run on Snowball 67B-A2B, the trainer resolved each rollout group's URI from an S3 archive holding 265 groups. One descriptor lookup took 4.1–4.6 s even after compaction had reduced `blobs` to 31 shards (80 MB); before compaction there were about 270 one-row shards. Resolving 56 groups did not finish within 1,800 s, and the run failed on its first training step. MarinSkyRL [#774](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/774) is replacing FineStore on that path with one S3 object per group.

Reproduce:

```python
import os, time
from finestore.reader import ReadView
from finestore.store import DataStore

root = "/tmp/finestore-point-lookup"
store = DataStore.open(root)
uris = []
for _ in range(400):
    with store.unbounded_transaction() as transaction:
        uris.append(transaction.write_object(f"rollouts/{len(uris)}", os.urandom(200_000)))
started = time.monotonic()
ReadView(root).resolve(uris[0])
print(time.monotonic() - started)  # grows linearly with the number of transactions
```

Done when:

- A primary-key lookup, including blob resolution, reads only shards whose key range can contain the key. Per-shard min/max primary key in the manifest would allow this.
- A reader can resolve many blob URIs in one pass over `blobs` and `_finestore_blob_parts`, instead of one scan per URI.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

`ReadView.point()` calls `scan()`, whose read plan opens the Parquet schema of every visible shard before the key filter runs. `open_blob()` does this for `blobs` and, for chunked payloads, repeats it for `_finestore_blob_parts`; the manifest records sequence bounds but no primary-key bounds. The open-PR preflight found no implementation for #9497.

**Relevant code**
- [`layout.py#L109-L128`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/b77516eb70fa5374cddf46c3ce180c18b99b3dac/lib/finestore/src/finestore/layout.py#L109-L128) — manifest shard fields
- [`reader.py#L266-L338`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/b77516eb70fa5374cddf46c3ce180c18b99b3dac/lib/finestore/src/finestore/reader.py#L266-L338) — schema reads and shard scans
- [`reader.py#L422-L502`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/b77516eb70fa5374cddf46c3ce180c18b99b3dac/lib/finestore/src/finestore/reader.py#L422-L502) — point and blob lookup chain
- [`store.py#L638-L664`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/b77516eb70fa5374cddf46c3ce180c18b99b3dac/lib/finestore/src/finestore/store.py#L638-L664) — flush-time shard metadata
- [`compaction.py#L103-L128`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/b77516eb70fa5374cddf46c3ce180c18b99b3dac/lib/finestore/src/finestore/compaction.py#L103-L128) — compaction output metadata

# Primary-key ranges and bulk blob resolution

A lookup should open only shards whose key bounds admit the requested key. A batch of blob URIs should reuse one pinned `ReadView` and scan each relevant table once. This keeps blobs in Parquet, as the [FineStore format decision](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/b77516eb70fa5374cddf46c3ce180c18b99b3dac/.agents/projects/finestore-format-hardening.md) requires.

## Challenges

Shard ranges can overlap after upserts or concurrent writes, so pruning cannot choose only one shard. Existing format-v2 manifests have no bounds, and nullable or unsupported key values need conservative handling to avoid dropping a matching row.

## Costs / Risks

- Bounds increase manifest size per shard and add small key-statistics work during writes and compaction.
- Existing archives need a one-time key-column read to gain pruning without rewriting payload columns.
- A `resolve_many()` result containing all payloads can use substantial memory; callers should batch large result sets or keep using `open_blob()` for streaming.

## Design

1. Add optional, typed min/max bounds for each primary-key column to `Shard`. Compute them from buffered rows in `DataTable._write()` and from the surviving rows during compaction. A missing bound means “unknown,” never “absent”; compare values under the column's Arrow type, and keep shards with null or incomparable bounds.
2. Select candidate shards from the pinned manifest **before** `_read_plan()` calls `pq.read_schema`. Apply this to equality and `in` predicates on primary-key columns, including the `name` prefix of the `(name, part)` key. Retain every overlapping candidate and the existing commit/sequence/generation deduplication rule. Leave broad scans unchanged; an absent point key returns `None` without opening a Parquet shard when all bounds exclude it.
3. Add `ReadView.resolve_many(uris: Sequence[str]) -> list[bytes | None]`, preserving input order and duplicate URIs. Validate references first, deduplicate requested names, fetch winning descriptors in one filtered pass over `blobs`, then fetch all required parts in one filtered pass over `_finestore_blob_parts`. Reuse the current missing-blob and `BlobCorruptionError` behavior, including part-count and size checks.
4. Add an explicit metadata backfill for existing manifests: read only primary-key columns from shards without bounds and publish a new manifest with the same shard paths through the existing HEAD compare-and-swap path. Readers conservatively scan unindexed shards until backfill completes. Keep read views pinned to their original manifest.

## Testing

Cover overlapping upserts, compaction, partial composite-key filters, absent keys, and old manifests without bounds. Cover mixed inline/chunked blobs, repeated and missing URIs, and corrupt parts. Count actual Parquet shard opens on local storage for 25, 100, and 400 shards, and compare lookup latency with the issue's baseline; the shard-open count for a single-blob lookup should depend on matching ranges, not total shard count.

## Open Questions

- Should the new bulk API also expose a streaming result form for callers whose requested blobs exceed memory? The proposed list preserves `resolve()` semantics and input order; `open_blob()` remains the bounded-memory path for individual blobs.

issues.title: [finestore] Point lookups read every shard of the table

issues.author: wind342
issues.body:
## Summary

I would like to test whether a training–learning–inference relation observed across several small neural systems survives at foundation-model scale.

The central hypothesis is not simply that post-update behavior can be predicted.

Rather, an actual optimizer update does not determine its functional effect by itself. Its target-specific response depends on the **receiving model state**, including the current parameter state and optimizer memory, together with the geometry of the realized update. Training then persistently reorganizes distributed functional support, and frozen inference subsequently recruits and combines that learned support without changing the persistent learned state.

This relation has already been tested under frozen protocols in a ~71M nanoGPT, ResNet/CIFAR, a diffusion U-Net, and a deterministic top-2 Vision MoE.

The main remaining axis is **scale**.

I would like to test the same relation first on a relatively inexpensive ~1B Marin language model, and, if it survives, repeat the experiment at a larger scale such as ~8B or an available MoE model.

A failure would be equally informative: the goal is to test whether scale exposes a counterexample.

## Existing MoE validation

The MoE experiment was designed as a falsification test rather than a performance benchmark.

It tested whether:

1. the same realized update produces different functional responses when applied to different receiving parameter states;
2. changing the receiving optimizer memory also changes the response;
3. finite-amplitude update responses are not necessarily linear;
4. target-boundary outcomes remain prospectively predictable from pre-update state and update geometry without reading post-update outputs;
5. actual training updates persistently reorganize distributed expert support;
6. frozen inference preserves persistent state while different queries recruit different routed supports;
7. expert contributions interact non-additively; and
8. rolling trained experts or the router back to their pre-learning versions changes the output, while restoring the trained versions restores the result.

All frozen training–learning and inference tests passed across three formal seeds in the executed top-2 Vision-MoE system.

The result is intentionally bounded to that system; it does not establish scale generalization.

## Proposed Marin test

At selected training updates:

1. seal the pre-update parameter and optimizer state;
2. record the actual optimizer-proposed update before inspecting its target response;
3. measure the same update under exchanged receiving states or optimizer memories;
4. probe the finite-amplitude response along the realized update direction;
5. test prospective target-response prediction using only pre-update information;
6. measure whether functional support is persistently reorganized by training;
7. at frozen checkpoints, test query-conditioned support recruitment, non-additive combination, learned-version dependence, and exact restoration.

The large-scale experiment should preserve the same basic causal structure as the existing frozen protocol, rather than reducing the test to a single prediction metric.

## Evaluation

The experiment would be considered supportive only if the main relation survives as a chain:

**receiving state + realized update → target-specific functional response → persistent support reorganization → frozen-inference use of the learned support.**

The individual intervention tests would be frozen before execution. Failed relations would be retained as counterevidence rather than reinterpreted after the run.

Prediction accuracy, transition recall, nonlinear response statistics, support reallocation, rollback effects, and compute/memory overhead would be reported as measurements of this relation, not as substitutes for it.

## Existing implementation

The small-scale experiments already include frozen protocols, state/update capture, receiving-state exchanges, finite-amplitude replay, prospective prediction, negative controls, support interventions, rollback tests, integrity checks, and independent verification.

Much of this infrastructure can be reused. The main work is adapting the measurements to Marin's training stack and making them practical at larger scale.

I am happy to handle the adaptation and analysis work.

If this fits Marin's research scope, I can provide the existing code and frozen MoE/nanoGPT results and start with a minimal ~1B-scale implementation before requesting a larger run.
issues.title: Experiment: Does the training–learning–inference relation survive at 1B–8B scale?

- The Marina runtime identity can access `projects/hai-gcp-models/secrets/HF_TOKEN/versions/3`.

spillover_issues.author: dlwh
spillover_issues.body:
## TL;DR

The Datakit SFT step-158000 checkpoint retains the isolated MRCR needle signal of its long-context step-157000 parent, but recovers less of that signal when distractors are present. On the same 299 two-shot examples, token-weighted needle recovery fell from 91.18% to 81.61% (paired bootstrap 95% interval for the drop: 8.16–11.08 percentage points). This is a teacher-forced retrieval diagnostic, not a generated MRCR accuracy score.

## Description

[Issue #8701](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8701) introduced a four-condition MRCR probe. Each condition scores the same gold response-body tokens: final query alone, query with the matching request/response pairs (needles), query with the other conversation turns (distractors), or the full conversation. The official worked examples and final query remain in every condition. The target is the selected earlier assistant response, even when that response contains a riddle or question.

We reran the probe on the native Datakit SFT step-158000 checkpoint behind the linked Hugging Face model and compared it with its longctx-skew4 step-157000 parent. The Hugging Face BF16 export was not evaluated; its numerical equivalence to the native checkpoint has not been established. Both artifacts have the same evaluation configuration and model-configuration hashes, 299 matching source IDs, all four finite condition losses, and 115,834 scored tokens. The run used a v4-64 TPU slice with CP8/EP4 and qk=1.75.

| Token-weighted metric | Parent step 157000 | SFT step 158000 | Change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Isolated needle gain, query only minus needle only | 1.39109 | 1.39205 | +0.00096 nats/token |
| Distracted needle gain, distractor only minus full context | 1.26838 | 1.13602 | -0.13235 nats/token |
| Needle recovery, distracted gain / isolated gain | 91.18% | 81.61% | -9.57 points |

A paired 10,000-resample bootstrap over source IDs gives a 95% interval of 8.16–11.08 points for the recovery drop and 0.11354–0.15194 nats/token for the distracted-gain drop. Recovery fell in each 2/4/8-needle and evidence-distance slice. These intervals describe sampling uncertainty on this fixed slice; they do not isolate which SFT data or training step caused the change.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Determine why the SFT checkpoint loses needle benefit in the presence of distractors while isolated needle gain remains stable. Check whether this behavior accounts for the low generated MRCR score, and identify which SFT stage or data mixture introduced it.

## Status

The parent/SFT likelihood comparison is complete. No causal ablation or matched generative error analysis has run yet.

## Links

- Hugging Face model card: https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.09.21
- Original probe and methodology: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8701
- SFT Iris run: https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fdlwh%2Fmrcr-datakit-sft-oracle4-20260928-r3
- SFT W&B: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mrcr-67b-step158000-qk175-datakit-sft-20260921-cap262144-two_shot-oracle4-v464cp8ep4
- SFT result artifact: `gs://marin-us-central2/eval/mrcr/datakit-sft-step158000/two_shot/cap-262144-v464cp8ep4-59e82a`
- Parent result artifact: `gs://marin-us-central2/eval/mrcr/qk175-longctx-skew4-step157000/two_shot/cap-262144-v464cp8ep4-433809`
- Evaluator revision: `3f77157789296a359433b792e0fd2001633b2bba`

## Decision Log

- Compare the SFT checkpoint with its actual longctx-skew4 parent on matching source IDs, instead of the separate qk=1.75 checkpoint reported in #8701.
- Use the four-condition likelihood probe to separate isolated needle availability from retrieval amid distractors.

## Conclusion

The isolated needle gain is unchanged at about 1.39 nats/token. The SFT checkpoint's distracted needle gain is lower by 0.13235 nats/token. This supports a distractor-interference regression in the likelihood probe; the cause and its relationship to generated MRCR failures remain open.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

Effort: low; reviewed the linked experiment issues, pinned evaluator and SFT recipe, and open MRCR PRs. The 299-source comparison shows a 9.57-point recovery drop with unchanged isolated needle gain, but these two checkpoints cannot locate the change within training or identify a data component. The [Datakit SFT run](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8954) is one 2,000-step continuation from the longctx-skew4 parent with 80% SFT and 20% pretraining replay. The generative comparison in [#8702](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8702) used a different step-157000 arm; [#9509](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9509) repairs sample-grade display, not aggregate scoring. No open PR covers this causal investigation.

**Relevant code**
- [`mrcr.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3f77157789296a359433b792e0fd2001633b2bba/experiments/datasets/mrcr.py#L336-L455) — four prompts, shared target tokens, source IDs.
- [`eval_mrcr_context.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3f77157789296a359433b792e0fd2001633b2bba/experiments/grug/moe/eval_mrcr_context.py#L646-L675) — paired token-weighted contrast.
- [`sft_datakit_chat_mix.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/77308d1a9fc61afd226f5cf98a6dabc14f1be39f/experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/sft_datakit_chat_mix.py#L36-L53) — parent and mixture settings.

# Proposed Fix

1. Match the existing four-condition artifacts by source ID and verify checkpoint, tokenizer, prompt, and scoring hashes. Recompute paired recovery and its interval from the saved rows. This is the fixed baseline for every subsequent comparison.
2. Compare generation from the *actual* longctx-skew4 parent and step-158000 on those same sources, with identical qk=1.75, prompt, context limit, decoding, and scorer. Reuse archived generations only where source IDs and settings match; otherwise run a bounded paired evaluation. Report canonical MRCR score, exact-prefix hit, nonce-stripped response similarity, empty/truncated outputs, and 2/4/8-needle and distance slices. Generate a separate needle-only counterfactual on the same sources to test whether removing distractors closes the checkpoint gap; label that arm noncanonical. If serving cannot fit the 262K slice, select a shared shorter subset and rerun the likelihood probe on that subset before comparing metrics.
3. Score available intermediate SFT checkpoints with the same four-condition probe to bracket the first recovery loss. If the generation result implicates distractors, reproduce the drop in the shortest continuation that does so, then compare the production 80/20 mixture with SFT-only and replay-only continuations from the same parent, seed, optimizer, and token budget. Follow with SFT source-family ablations only if the first comparison implicates SFT data.

Attribute the loss to a data component only if its controlled ablation restores distracted needle gain while isolated gain stays stable. Treat a generated-score link as supported only if the paired full-versus-needle-only generation contrast moves in the same direction after SFT; otherwise record the likelihood regression and generation failure as separate findings. Publish per-source results, intervals, exact configs, checkpoint IDs, and run links in this issue and the research logbook.

spillover_issues.author: ClassicLarry
spillover_issues.body:
🤖 **Marin Belay Intake: post research suggestions for [Marin Belay v1 (#9451)](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451) here.**

Marin Belay is an agent-run experiment loop that hill-climbs the grug `fast_track` scaling ladder (Paloma macro loss, fixed 8-minute 8×H100 budget). The agent reads and acts only on the main thread (#9451), which is limited to users with write access. Suggestions from anyone else come in through this issue:

1. **Post your suggestion as a comment here.** One idea per comment, with a paper link or a short rationale if you have one.
2. **A maintainer reviews it.** When a member of the `marin-devs` team reacts with 👍, an automated workflow (every ~5 minutes) copies the comment verbatim into #9451, attributed to you and linked back here.
3. **The workflow then adds 🚀 to your comment**, meaning it has been transferred. It transfers each comment once; editing a comment after the 🚀 does not re-send it.

Suggestions that are off-topic, duplicate existing work, or ask the agent to do anything other than ML research on the ladder won't be approved. The main thread's Status section lists what has been tried and the current best recipe.
