spillover_issues.author: timodonnell
spillover_issues.body:
On marin GPU training (`--extra gpu`, CoreWeave H100 `cw-rno2a`), levanter dense-LM attention runs **non-fused**, leaving significant throughput on the table at long sequence lengths.

## Root cause — a backend/dependency mismatch
- levanter's default GPU attention backend is `AttentionBackend.NVTE` (Transformer Engine), but the `gpu` extra ships **`flash-attn-4[cu13]`**, not `transformer_engine`. So NVTE hits `transformer_engine is not installed … Falling back to the reference implementation` (`levanter/layers/attention.py`) — a non-fused O(seq²) kernel that also OOMs at seq 8192.
- `AttentionBackend.JAX_FLASH` avoids the OOM but is an XLA-fusion blocked-flash (memory-safe, not a fused CUDA kernel).
- The **`flash-attn-4`** that the `gpu` extra installs has **no levanter backend wired to it** (enum: `{DEFAULT, NVTE, SPLASH, JAX_FLASH, VANILLA}`; `attention.py` never imports `flash_attn`). So the fused library marin ships is dead weight for dense-LM training.

## Evidence (from MarinFold exp108 — 3B Qwen3, seq 8192, 8×H100)
- The TE-not-installed fallback warning on the default backend.
- A perfetto trace of a real run (`jax_flash`): attention appears only as XLA `gemm_fusion_dot` + `exp`/`reduce` softmax fusions — no fused/flash/pallas/TE kernel. ~25% of GPU compute time is reduce/softmax, ~45% is non-GEMM.
- OOM (`RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED`, 64 GiB score matrix) with the reference path at batch 128 × seq 8192.

## Ask
Provide a working fused-attention path for levanter **dense-LM** GPU training. Two options:
1. **Wire a levanter attention backend to the `flash-attn-4` marin already ships** (preferred — it's installed, avoids adding a heavy dep), or
2. Add `transformer_engine` to the `gpu` extra so the existing NVTE default works.

## Impact
Any levanter dense-LM GPU run on marin. Concretely, MarinFold's first GPU sweep is training with non-fused attention: Open-Athena/MarinFold#108.

comments.author: timodonnell
comments.body:
🤖

# Research

Confirmed: `default_attention_type()` returns NVTE on GPU, but the gpu extra ships `flash-attn-4` + `nvidia-cutlass-dsl` and not `transformer_engine`, so the default warns and drops to the unfused path. Levanter already has a differentiable FA4/CuTe JAX binding in grug (custom-VJP backward, bf16/fp16 causal self-attention, GQA, packed segment ids via per-token lower bounds, sliding window, SM80/90/100/120) with fwd+grad parity tests against reference — it just isn't reachable from `dot_product_attention`.

**Relevant code**
- [`attention.py#L82-L89`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/layers/attention.py#L82-L89) - GPU default = NVTE
- [`attention.py#L415-L506`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/layers/attention.py#L415-L506) - `_try_te_attention` fallback contract (warn → None → blocked JAX flash)
- [`_fa4_cute_backend.py#L652-L750`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/_fa4_cute_backend.py#L652-L750) - differentiable FA4 kernel boundary (`jax.custom_vjp`)
- [`_fa4_cute.py#L149-L170`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/_fa4_cute.py#L149-L170) - causal/packed/sliding-window → `lower_bounds`/`valid` lowering
- [`lib/levanter/pyproject.toml#L90`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/pyproject.toml#L90) - gpu extra already ships flash-attn-4 + cutlass-dsl

# Proposed Fix

Option 1 (wire the shipped flash-attn-4), all in `levanter/layers/attention.py`:

- Add `AttentionBackend.FA4 = "fa4"`. `default_attention_type()` returns FA4 on GPU when `flash_attn` + `cutlass` are importable, else NVTE (TE installs keep today's behavior).
- Add `_try_fa4_attention(...)` mirroring `_try_te_attention`: bin NamedArray axes to BSHD with the existing `_bin_and_group_axes_by_function`, lower the layers `AttentionMask` (`is_causal` + `segment_ids` + `sliding_window`) to FA4 `lower_bounds`/`valid` via the existing grug helpers, and `shard_map` `fa4_cute_attention_forward(..., sm_scale=scaling_factor)` with haliax physical pspecs (splash-style; batch/head sharding OK, sequence must be unsharded).
- Unsupported configs (dropout>0, bias, `logits_soft_cap`, `attn_sink`, `causal_offset`, explicit/non-causal mask, cross-attention, non-bf16/fp16, unsupported arch) warn once and return None → existing memory-safe blocked JAX flash; explicit `attn_backend: fa4` raises instead.
- No dependency changes; grug FA4 entry points get public exports (hoisting to `levanter/kernels/` can follow separately).

Rejected: `transformer_engine` in the gpu extra (heavy, tightly version-coupled to jax/CUDA; nothing tracks jax 0.10 reliably); `jax.nn.dot_product_attention(implementation="cudnn")` (no packed segment_ids, and packing is the common dense-LM path); the FA4 THD variant (head_dim-128-only, rejects MHA, sliding window unimplemented on SM90).

Tests: CPU — mask→lower-bounds lowering + fallback/forced-raise dispatch; GPU-gated — fwd+grad parity of `dot_product_attention(attn_backend=fa4)` vs reference across MHA/GQA/packing/sliding-window (mirroring `tests/grug/test_fa4_cute_attention.py`). Validation: dense-LM step at seq 8192 on H100 with no fallback warning and the fused kernel visible in the trace.

Note: I did not use `levanter_flash_patch.zip` from the earlier comment — an opaque patch archive from an unaffiliated account shouldn't be applied; maintainers may want to hide that comment.

comments.author: timodonnell
comments.body: 🤖 Fix up at #7015: adds `AttentionBackend.FA4` wired to the grug FA4/CuTe segmented kernels and makes it the GPU default when the `gpu` extra's `flash-attn-4`/`nvidia-cutlass-dsl` are importable (NVTE otherwise). Validated on a cw-rno2a H100 pod: fwd+grad parity vs reference across MHA/GQA/packed-segments/sliding-window at 7e-2 tolerance, and 3.4× faster than the `jax_flash` fallback on this issue's shape (seq 8192, GQA 32/8, head_dim 128, bf16: 11.3 ms vs 38.9 ms fwd+bwd per iteration, single GPU).

spillover_issues.author: rjpower
spillover_issues.body:
https://marin.community/ is sorely out of date with the example experiments.

Let's make this a non-issue: can we make it so that a new experiment starts out with an issue template, and then we have an agent process which reaps these issues nightly and creates concise documentation and blog teasers? We can build on the wandb statistics and any comments tracked in the issue to give users an insight into what we're up to.

An experiment needn't be closed out - we could show ongoing and finished experiments, the author, etc.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Status:** Analysis only — this is a multi-module feature (issue template + nightly automation + doc/blog generation), larger than a self-contained fix, so handing back a proposed approach for human review before implementation.

# Research

Most of the requested machinery already exists in pieces; the gap is a GitHub-native experiment template, a generation step that turns reaped issues into newcomer-facing docs/teasers, and a workflow that actually runs the nightly reap on schedule.

**Relevant code**
- [`.agents/skills/scrub-experiment-issue-tldrs/SKILL.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/.agents/skills/scrub-experiment-issue-tldrs/SKILL.md) — already reaps `experiment` issues nightly and maintains `<!-- experiment-tldr:start/end -->` summary blocks. Has `schedule_cron: "0 8 * * *"` but it is **not wired to anything**.
- [`infra/pre-commit.py#L718-L724`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/pre-commit.py#L718-L724) — the *only* consumer of `schedule_cron`/`schedule_tz`: it validates them, nothing executes them.
- [`.github/workflows/ops-nightshift-doc-drift.yaml`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/.github/workflows/ops-nightshift-doc-drift.yaml) + [`infra/cron/nightshift_doc_drift.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/cron/nightshift_doc_drift.py) — the established "nightly agent" pattern (workflow on `cron` → script invokes `claude --model=opus` with an app token, opens PRs/issues, no self-credit).
- [`scripts/pm/itemize_experiment_issues.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/scripts/pm/itemize_experiment_issues.py) + [`.agents/skills/organize-experiments/SKILL.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/.agents/skills/organize-experiments/SKILL.md) — already harvest `experiment`-labeled issues into [`docs/reports/index.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/docs/reports/index.md), resolving W&B run names via `wandb.Api()`.
- [`.agents/skills/file-issue/SKILL.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/.agents/skills/file-issue/SKILL.md) (experiment body, ~L55-83) — the experiment issue body template (TL;DR / Hypothesis / Status / Links / Decision Log / Conclusion) lives in a skill, **not** as a GitHub form. There is no `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/` directory.

**Gaps vs. the ask:** (1) no GitHub-native experiment template so humans/agents get the structure for free; (2) the nightly reaper isn't scheduled — `schedule_cron` is decorative; (3) no step that emits concise newcomer docs / blog teasers (only TL;DR blocks on the issue itself and a link index); (4) no surface (blog / recent-experiments page) showing ongoing vs. finished + author.

# Proposed Approach

Build on what exists rather than adding a parallel system. Four increments, each independently reviewable:

1. **GitHub-native experiment template** (`.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/experiment.yml` + `config.yml`). Mirror the `file-issue` experiment body (TL;DR, Hypothesis/Goal, Status, Links: Logbook/W&B/PRs, Decision Log, Conclusion) and auto-apply the `experiment` label. This is the small, self-contained "template" piece and the natural first PR — but it should still be reviewed for field wording first. Keep `file-issue/SKILL.md` as the source of truth; the form references it.

2. **Wire the nightly reaper.** Add `.github/workflows/ops-nightshift-experiment-docs.yaml` + `infra/cron/nightshift_experiment_docs.py` following the doc-drift pattern (app token, `claude --model=opus`, attribution disabled). It runs the existing `scrub-experiment-issue-tldrs` + `organize-experiments` skills. Recommend keeping `schedule_cron` advisory (hand-author the workflow, as today) rather than adding a metadata→workflow generator — it matches existing practice and avoids a meta-layer.

3. **Generation step → newcomer docs/teasers.** Extend the reaper to emit a short teaser per recently-updated experiment (title, author, ongoing/finished, one-paragraph TL;DR, top W&B numbers via the `itemize` script's existing `wandb.Api()` path, links) into a new `docs/reports/recent-experiments.md` (or `docs/blog/`), surfaced in `mkdocs.yml`. This is the bulk of the new code and the main design decision: dedicated blog dir vs. an auto-generated section in the existing report index.

4. **Author/status metadata.** Derive author from issue creator and ongoing/finished from issue state + a `tldr`/conclusion signal; render in the teaser page.

**Open questions for a human before implementation:**
- Blog teasers as a new `docs/blog/` surface, or an auto-generated section in `docs/reports/index.md`?
- Should generated teasers land as auto-merge PRs (like doc-drift) or be committed directly?
- Is publishing to the public `marin.community` site in scope, or only the in-repo MkDocs docs?
- Keep `schedule_cron` advisory (hand-authored workflows) or build a metadata→workflow generator?

I can take #1 (the issue template) as a first small PR once the field wording is confirmed; the rest should wait on the design answers above.

spillover_issues.author: ravwojdyla-agent
spillover_issues.body:
## Description

Add a DaemonSet-equivalent primitive to Iris: **run exactly one instance of a workload on every node of a category, for that node's lifetime**, automatically tracking autoscaler churn. Iris can schedule discrete jobs but cannot express "one per node of scale group S" — constraints are positive-match only and coscheduling `group_by` is the opposite (gang affinity), so there is no spread/anti-affinity operator today.

Motivating consumer: smallquery's warm worker fleet (#6761), which must cover every preemptible VM. Generalizes to node-local log shippers, metric exporters, and cache/proxy sidecars.

Design + research + spec: `.agents/projects/iris_daemon/{design.md,research.md,spec.md}` (design-doc PR forthcoming).

Approach (Route A, committed v1):
- `DaemonSpec` declared in cluster YAML (sibling to `scale_groups:`), selector = a scale group + optional constraints.
- Controller-side `DaemonReconciler` maintains "one running daemon task per matching live worker" by **pinning each instance to a worker id** (HARD constraint) — sidesteps the missing spread operator — and reuses the autoscaler's worker join/leave signal. Node loss tears down for free via task↔worker binding; reconciler only ever creates.
- Discovery via EndpointService (`<endpoint_name>/<worker_id>` prefix); supervision/health/preemption accounting inherited because a daemon is a task.
- Recommended opportunistic shape: BATCH band + zero `cpu_millicores` + hard `memory_bytes`.
- Read-only `DaemonService` proto (`ListDaemons`/`GetDaemon`); `iris daemon list/status` CLI.

Out of scope v1: Route B bootstrap sidecar (`WorkerConfig.sidecar_containers`), dynamic RPC-created daemons, cross-scale-group selectors, rolling updates.

### Definition of Done

- [ ] Design-doc PR merged (`.agents/projects/iris_daemon/`); resource-accounting policy (`reserve_memory`) blessed by Iris owners
- [ ] `DaemonSpec` config + `DaemonReconciler` maintain the one-per-matching-worker invariant
- [ ] Reconciler unit tests pass across worker add/remove/restart and spec add/change/delete
- [ ] Churn integration test on an Iris dev cluster: scale up/down + kick instances, fleet re-converges, endpoints reflect live set
- [ ] `DaemonService` status RPCs + `iris daemon` CLI land
- [ ] Works on GCP/TPU and k8s/CoreWeave backends

spillover_issues.author: ravwojdyla-agent
spillover_issues.body:
## Description

["Hubs or Fringes: Pretraining Data Selection via Web Graph Centrality"](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.11499) (Badoni, Chen, Wang) proposes using web-graph centrality — PageRank, betweenness, Katz — computed over the crawl hyperlink graph as a pretraining data-selection signal. Documents from high-centrality "hub" pages are prioritized over "fringe" pages; the authors report downstream benchmark gains over random and fringe-based selection.

Open question: **should we compute a centrality feature for our documents and use it in the next data mix?**

Things to scope before committing:
- Do we retain the hyperlink graph (source/outlink structure) needed to compute centrality, or only extracted text? Centrality requires the graph, which most text-only pipelines discard.
- Cost/feasibility of building a web-scale link graph and running PageRank/Katz at our corpus scale.
- How a centrality score would compose with our existing quality classifiers — additive signal vs. redundant with what fasttext/Luxical-style filters already capture.
- A small ablation: tag a sample with centrality buckets and check correlation with existing quality scores and with downstream eval, before any full-mix integration.

### Definition of Done

- Decision recorded (adopt / reject / needs-experiment) with rationale.
- If adopt or needs-experiment: a concrete plan for (a) where the link graph comes from, (b) which centrality metric, (c) how the feature enters the data-mix selection, and (d) the ablation that would justify inclusion.

spillover_issues.author: dlwh
spillover_issues.body:
## Background
In #6070, the [PPL circuit-coverage gap dashboard](https://marin.community/analysis/ppl-circuit-coverage-gap/) showed Marin 32B lagging Qwen3 32B on short deterministic continuations: arithmetic, string/token manipulation, exact character tracking, and literal formatting. #6236 tracks adding new task families, but existing tasks also need more surface diversity so models do not overfit a single prompt shape.

## Description
Add compact template variants for existing `experiments/evals/ppl_circuit_coverage_v2.py` tasks. This is intended as a bounded contributor task: pick one existing task, add several alternate surface forms, inspect local samples, and verify target-only supervised formatting still holds.

The goal is not to add scaffolding. Keep examples Tufte-style: completed few-shot lines followed by one held-out completion prefix. Avoid labels such as `Family:`, `Task:`, `Prompt:`, `worked examples`, `held-out query`, `answer:`, or `Final answer:`.

Example target shape:

```text
text = "abcdef"; text[1:5:2] -> 'bd'
text = "marin"; text[0:4:1] -> 'mari'
text = "́kder/ejehcp"; text[6:11:1] -> 
```

with supervised `output` containing only:

```text
'ejehc'
```

Good first template-diversity targets:

- `string_slicing`: Python slice notation, prose-light `slice(text,start,stop,step)`, table-like `text | start | stop | step ->`.
- `json_field_reemit`: dot paths, bracket paths, compact `object/path -> value`.
- `csv_tsv_transforms`: delimiter names, visible separators, quoted-field variants.
- `carry_addition` / `borrow_subtraction`: vertical arithmetic, inline arithmetic, digit-array forms.
- `line_column_offsets`: `line:col`, JSON object, and compact tuple surfaces.
- `markdown_table_padding` / `outline_indentation`: vary content while preserving exact final formatting.

Suggested workflow:

1. Pick one existing task from `PPL_CIRCUIT_COVERAGE_V2_SLICES`.
2. Add a small set of surface templates inside that task's generator or a local helper.
3. Keep metadata sufficient to recompute the target independently.
4. Generate local samples:
   `uv run python -c 'from experiments.evals.ppl_circuit_coverage_v2 import write_local_sample; write_local_sample("/tmp/ppl_circuit_v2_sample", examples_per_config=36)'`
5. Inspect at least 36 examples for the task. Check ambiguity, target leakage, escaping, and accidental task telegraphing.
6. Run:
   `uv run --with pytest --with pytest-timeout pytest -m "not slow" tests/evals/test_ppl_circuit_coverage_v2.py -q`
7. Include five representative before/after examples in the PR description.

### Definition of Done
- One existing task has at least five compact surface variants, or a clear rationale for fewer variants if the task is format-constrained.
- Generated local samples show the variants are actually used.
- Supervised `input` ends before the held-out answer, and `output` contains only the final answer plus newline.
- Tests cover no target leakage and no banned scaffold strings for the changed task.
- The PR links this issue and includes five representative generated examples.

spillover_issues.author: Helw150
spillover_issues.body:
🤖 _Reworked by an agent (William's session). Original title/scope: "Test Qwen 2.5 Base on David's PPL sets, Correlate with Coder Models SWE-Bench Perf." — generalized below; the coder/SWE-bench instance is retained as a planned extension._

## Hypothesis

A base model's **perplexity (bits-per-byte) on a target skill's reasoning traces** predicts how good that model becomes **after post-training** on that skill — before running any post-training. If true, base-model PPL on the right distribution is a cheap screen for "will this base respond to RL/SFT on skill X."

This is the mechanistic version of the SimpleRL-Zoo finding ("Qwen bases respond to zero-RL, Llama/Mistral don't"): the base that already compresses the reasoning-trace distribution best is the one post-training can most easily amplify.

## What we ran this session (math / SimpleRL-Zoo instance)

- **Eval set:** new `math_reasoning` PPL bundle — `nvidia/OpenMathReasoning` `cot` + `tir` splits (verified long CoT math traces), target-only BPB, 256 docs/split, 4096 ctx. Built in David's perplexity-gap format.
- **Models:** the 10 SimpleRL-Zoo base models (Qwen2.5 0.5B–32B, Qwen2.5-Math-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, DeepSeek-Math-7B, Mistral-7B-v0.1, Mistral-Small-24B).
- **Where:** scored in-process via Levanter on a v5p-8 dev TPU.
- **Correlated against:** the published SimpleRL-Zoo post-training accuracy table (avg over GSM8K / MATH500 / Minerva / Olympiad / AIME24 / AMC23).

### Result (n=10)

![Base-model PPL vs post-SimpleRL accuracy (n=10, r=-0.89)](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/Helw150/fca0e45e3fa10b7d0c0a8ecb4c79fbfa/raw/simplerl_corr.png)

_Interactive version (Plotly scatter with cot/tir + base/post toggles and a 7–8B-cohort filter) lives in `experiments/score_simplerl_math_reasoning_ppl.py`'s companion viewer (`simplerl_viewer/index.html`, served locally during the session)._

| Predictor | → post-SimpleRL Avg |
|---|---|
| base **cot** BPB | Pearson r = **−0.89**, Spearman ρ = −0.87 |
| base **tir** BPB | Pearson r = **−0.92**, Spearman ρ = −0.87 |
| within 7–8B cohort (cot) | Pearson r = **−0.97** |

Lower base BPB on the reasoning traces ⇒ higher post-RL math accuracy. Holds across n=7→10 as points landed; strongest within a fixed size band (removes the size confound).

| Model | base cot BPB | base Avg | +SimpleRL Avg |
|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen2.5-32B | 0.402 | 45.9 | 61.9 |
| Qwen2.5-14B | 0.418 | 43.2 | 56.8 |
| Mistral-Small-24B | 0.430 | 27.6 | 49.6 |
| Qwen2.5-7B | 0.440 | 40.3 | 55.2 |
| Qwen2.5-Math-7B | 0.443 | 37.2 | 59.5 |
| DeepSeek-Math-7B | 0.494 | 11.3 | 29.2 |
| Llama-3.1-8B | 0.495 | 10.6 | 22.0 |
| Qwen2.5-1.5B | 0.504 | 18.5 | 36.1 |
| Mistral-7B-v0.1 | 0.523 | 5.3 | 18.6 |
| Qwen2.5-0.5B | 0.587 | 12.1 | 20.9 |

## Artifacts produced

- `experiments/evals/math_reasoning_ppl.py` — `math_reasoning` validation sets (OpenMathReasoning cot/tir), registered as a bundle in `experiments/evals/perplexity_gap_registry.py`.
- `experiments/exp_simplerl_base_math_reasoning_ppl.py` — executor experiment scoring the 10 base models on the bundle (one Iris TPU job per model).
- `experiments/score_simplerl_math_reasoning_ppl.py` — lightweight dev-TPU scorer (one model per subprocess, clears HF cache between models to fit disk).
- **Levanter fix:** `lib/levanter/src/levanter/models/mistral.py` — `MistralConfig` now honors an explicit `head_dim` (read it in `from_hf_config`, use it in `HeadSize` and `attention_config`). Required to load Mistral-Small-24B (head_dim=128 ≠ hidden/heads); backward-compatible no-op when `head_dim` is None. `LlamaConfig.from_hf_config` has the same gap — worth a follow-up.
- `scripts/iris/dev_tpu.py` — added `--priority` flag to `allocate`.

## Caveats

- Predicts **level** (base and post-RL accuracy), not the **gain** (delta is noisy w.r.t. BPB).
- Across all sizes the −0.89 is partly the size confound (bigger ⇒ lower BPB everywhere); the within-cohort −0.97 is the cleaner cross-architecture signal.
- n is small.
- base-BPB → base-accuracy is near-tautological; the non-obvious result is base-BPB → **post-RL** accuracy.

## Next steps

1. **More David PPL sets** — run the same 10 base models on additional bundles and compare per-bundle correlation:
   - *signal:* `synthetic_reasoning` (StepMath + algorithmic; needs a 3-line bundle wrapper), `code_interpretation`, `ppl_circuit_coverage_v2`.
   - *control:* `base_raw` (Paloma + uncheatable) — generic-text BPB should predict math-RL outcome **weakly**; that's what shows the predictor is reasoning-distribution-specific, not generic LM quality.
2. **Post-trained BPB** — score the 10 `hkust-nlp/*-SimpleRL-Zoo` checkpoints on the same traces to correlate base-BPB ↔ post-BPB directly (not just vs published accuracy).
3. **Original coder/SWE-bench instance** — score Qwen2.5(-Coder) bases' PPL on code-reasoning/SWE traces and correlate with Coder-model SWE-bench performance, mirroring the math result.
4. Commit/PR the artifacts above; consider upstreaming the Levanter `head_dim` fix.

comments.author: Helw150
comments.body:
🤖 Session summary — extended the base-PPL → post-RL study to a full exploitation/exploration decomposition and a semantic-branching metric. All numbers below are the 10 SimpleRL-Zoo base models, scored on a v5p-8 via Levanter, targets = the published SimpleRL-Zoo accuracy table.

## 1. Exploitation — correct-solution NLL (BPB)
Base BPB on the verified OpenMathReasoning `cot`/`tir` traces *is* the correct-solution NLL. It predicts post-RL math accuracy:
- `cot` → post-RL Avg: **r = −0.89**; `tir` → **r = −0.92**; within the 7–8B cohort **r = −0.97**.

**Distribution-specificity** (added `synthetic_reasoning` = StepMath + algorithmic/CLRS, 32 slices): real math traces predict post-RL far better than templated synthetic reasoning — `cot` −0.89 vs `synth` −0.68…−0.72 (StepMath best, CLRS worst). The predictor is specific to the *target* distribution, not "reasoning-shaped" text.

**PPL vs the pre-RL metric**: base PPL beats pre-RL accuracy at predicting post-RL **exactly where the benchmark saturates/floors** — GSM8K (|r| 0.98 vs 0.74), Minerva (0.92 vs 0.85), AIME24 avg@32 (0.84 vs 0.79). On clean mid-difficulty metrics (MATH500/Olympiad/AMC) the pre-RL number wins.

## 2. Exploration — does adding a policy-spread term help?
Computed per-target-token, same forward pass: token entropy `H`, `p_top`/`branch_mass`, renormalized-tail entropy, and an **embedding effective-rank** (participation ratio of the policy-weighted top-k *output-embedding* cloud — "semantic branching", which ignores syntactic synonyms that token entropy over-counts).

- **Token entropy is ~redundant with BPB** (collinearity +0.93). A confident model is peaked on the correct token *and* peaked overall.
- **Embedding effective-rank is less redundant** (collinearity +0.78) and adds real signal: the joint model `post_+RL ~ BPB + emb_rank` gives **R² = 0.931 (adj 0.91)** vs BPB-only 0.797 (adj 0.77). `emb_rank` β = −67, **t = −3.68, p = 0.008**; model F(2,7) = 47, p = 0.0001. **LOO-CV RMSE drops 10.6 → 6.7** acc-pts (out-of-sample improvement → not just overfitting an extra knob).
- Sign is **negative**: at matched BPB, *more* semantic branching → *worse* post-RL. So even the cleaner "semantic" metric leans toward decisiveness/clarity, not "exploration helps."

## 3. The deflating caveat — it predicts capability *level*, not RL-friendliness
RL adds a near-constant **+15.8 ± 4.1** pts to everyone, so **base and post-RL accuracy are 0.97 correlated**. Consequences:
- Predicting base vs +RL is the same problem (joint R² 0.923 vs 0.931) — the base/+RL toggle is cosmetic.
- Predicting the **RL gain** (post − base) **fails: R² = 0.33**, and `emb_rank` *hurts* adj-R² there.

So this work shows base PPL (+ semantic effective-rank) forecast **math-capability level**, which RL preserves — **not** *which weak base benefits most from RL*. The gain stays largely unexplained.

## Honest limitations
n = 10, and the models aren't independent (≈3 families × a size ladder, with a strong scale confound), so OLS p-values are optimistic — treat as suggestive, not established. Metrics are teacher-forced on *correct* traces at T=1 (a proxy for free-sampling exploration); the real exploration signal is sequence-level / correct-vs-incorrect separation. Target is the published post-RL **Avg**, not measured pass@K. `emb_rank` used k=16 / output embeddings.

## Artifacts (branch, uncommitted)
- `experiments/evals/math_reasoning_ppl.py` + `synthetic_reasoning` bundle in `perplexity_gap_registry.py`
- `experiments/exp_simplerl_base_math_reasoning_ppl.py` (executor) and `experiments/score_simplerl_math_reasoning_ppl.py` (lightweight dev-TPU scorer, `--metric nll|entropy`)
- Levanter `compute_target_entropy` (entropy, p_top, tail, **emb_eff_rank**) in `lib/levanter/.../main/perplexity_gap.py`; plus a `MistralConfig` `head_dim` fix (needed to load Mistral-Small-24B)
- `scripts/iris/dev_tpu.py` `--priority` flag
- Interactive monitor (lenses × per-benchmark/base/+RL/gain targets, pre-RL-vs-PPL scoreboard, sigmoid + joint BPB+emb_rank fit with floored predictions, live R²/adj-R²/LOO).

## Suggested next steps
1. Validate against **measured pass@K**, not the published Avg.
2. More base models / independent families to break the size confound (cluster- or family-held-out fits).
3. Sequence-level exploration (distinct-answer diversity, or silhouette clarity on a static AIME rollout set) to actually target the *gain*.

spillover_issues.body:
A SkyRL experiment can select a custom Harbor environment with `terminal_bench.harbor.import_path`. The locked SkyRL task environment does not include the selected package. `SkyRLRuntime` supplies only a runtime commit and dependency profile. Thus, a Marin experiment cannot use `shellbox.backends.shellsim.environment:ShellSimEnvironment` without a new MarinSkyRL lock and image.

Reproduce:
1. Pin MarinSkyRL commit `fbfa158d4caf7003d5fe64d58f4faf5c600ec156` with the `megatron` profile.
2. Set `terminal_bench.harbor.import_path` to `shellbox.backends.shellsim.environment:ShellSimEnvironment`.
3. Start the Harbor runner. The runtime cannot import `shellbox` because its `pyproject.toml` and `uv.lock` contain neither `marin-shellbox` nor `shellsim`.

Expected: `SkyRLRuntime` can declare pinned task-environment packages, or a locked profile includes Shellbox with ShellSim.

Issue #9528 uses a temporary workaround. Its data artifact adds the pinned pure-Python modules to `PYTHONPATH`. Remove that workaround after this issue has a locked runtime path.

spillover_issues.author: ravwojdyla-agent
spillover_issues.body:
A simulated Python subprocess with an infinite loop exhausts the parent `Environment` CPU limit before either `subprocess.run(timeout=...)` or the `timeout` command stops it. A verifier cannot convert a nonterminating candidate program into an ordinary failed test. The whole ShellSim trial terminates with `stop_reason='cpu_exhausted'`.

Reproduce:
1. Install `shellsim==0.1.20`.
2. Create `Environment(cpu=10_000_000)`.
3. Run `timeout 0.01 /usr/bin/python -c 'while True: pass'`.
4. Observe return code 137, `stop_reason='cpu_exhausted'`, and `environment.terminated == True`.

The same result occurs when a simulated Python verifier calls `subprocess.run(..., timeout=0.01)` around the candidate.

Expected: a child-process timeout stops the child before it exhausts the parent environment. The verifier stays live and can record a failed test.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

With `shellsim==0.1.20` and a fresh `Environment(cpu=10_000_000)` for each command, both `timeout 0.01 /usr/bin/python -c 'while True: pass'` and a simulated Python `subprocess.run(..., timeout=0.01)` return 137 with `stop_reason='cpu_exhausted'` and `terminated=True`; the Shellbox adapter raises `RuntimeError` for the first command. ShellSim's command timeout and Python child wait use virtual deadlines, but its scheduler advances to the next timer only after runnable work stops; the loop remains runnable until the shared CPU budget is exhausted.

**Relevant code**
- [machine.py#L95-L122](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/4aa26ec73d248b974766f8940a896a8c888d8269/lib/shellbox/src/shellbox/backends/shellsim/machine.py#L95-L122) - terminated environment becomes an error.
- [exec.rs#L2950-L2975](https://github.com/rjpower/shellsim/blob/2b9f0ccaf257c33ded607e2becbe62157e1e3d13/src/exec.rs#L2950-L2975) - virtual clock advances after runnable work stops.
- [timeout.rs#L73-L83](https://github.com/rjpower/shellsim/blob/2b9f0ccaf257c33ded607e2becbe62157e1e3d13/src/program/timeout.rs#L73-L83) - command timeout waits on a deadline.
- [process.rs#L126-L151](https://github.com/rjpower/shellsim/blob/2b9f0ccaf257c33ded607e2becbe62157e1e3d13/src/python/process.rs#L126-L151) - Python wait checks its deadline.
- [time_virtualization.rs#L328-L342](https://github.com/rjpower/shellsim/blob/2b9f0ccaf257c33ded607e2becbe62157e1e3d13/tests/time_virtualization.rs#L328-L342) - existing timeout test uses a sleeping child.

# Proposed Fix

`ShellSimEnvironment.exec()` → `ShellSimMachine.run()` → `shellsim.Environment.run()` reaches ShellSim's scheduler, so the fix requires an upstream release followed by a Marin dependency update.

1. Add upstream regressions for both timeout forms with `while True: pass`; give the environment enough CPU for the timeout and a follow-up command, then assert exit 124 or `TimeoutExpired` and a successful `echo ok` in the same environment.
2. Advance modeled monotonic time deterministically between bounded runnable quanta when deadlines exist, then process due events before dispatching more child work; preserve the existing clock behavior for runs without deadlines.
3. Release ShellSim, update [Shellbox's minimum version](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/4aa26ec73d248b974766f8940a896a8c888d8269/lib/shellbox/pyproject.toml#L15) and lockfile, and add an adapter regression that runs a timed-out verifier followed by another command in the same trial.

spillover_issues.author: yonromai
spillover_issues.body:
## TL;DR

- **Decision:** Should an Iris Kubernetes job be able to require one specific NVLink rack?
- **Need:** `group_by="nvlink.domain"` keeps a gang in one rack but does not choose which rack. A job limited to rack 392 needs to name it.
- **Current gap:** Iris skips that exact-rack constraint when building a Kubernetes Pod and lowercases the case-sensitive rack label before serialization.
- **Proposal:** [Draft PR #9478](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9478) would let a job require `nvlink.domain == "DH1-392-US-EAST-08A"`. The job could not run on another rack if the requested rack is missing or full.
- **Scope:** This feature would not reserve Hero training racks or prevent Batch jobs from using spare nodes there.

A read-only audit on September 26 found three Batch jobs using 24 GPUs on six other nodes in three of Hero's 11 training racks. It found no GPU double-booking and did not measure training harm. No placement with the changed controller has been tested live.

<details>
<summary>Evidence: placement audit, current code, and a local test failure</summary>

**Placement audit.** Iris controller `task_attempts` showed Hero using 16 nodes on each of 11 racks (176 four-GPU tasks). Racks 124, 125, and 129 each had 18 labeled nodes: 16 used by Hero and two by one Batch job. Captured Kubernetes node labels mapped the nodes to racks; FineLog `iris.profile` samples confirmed the Batch tasks ran there. The audit did not compare training speed with and without Batch work. A separate job requested only `group_by="nvlink.domain"`, so its placement did not test an exact-rack request.

**Actual rack label.** The captured Kubernetes node snapshot included `s1mwxs64` with `ds.coreweave.com/nvlink.domain=DH1-392-US-EAST-08A`. The uppercase characters matter for an exact label match.

**Current code.** [Gang topology](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/562d705673859548c58b46d8f2383ab8a053797f/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py#L285-L292) selects the `nvlink.domain` level without a rack value. The [Pod selector mapping](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/562d705673859548c58b46d8f2383ab8a053797f/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py#L179-L183) lists only `pool` and `region`; [unknown keys are skipped](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/562d705673859548c58b46d8f2383ab8a053797f/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py#L335-L346). [String constraints are lowercased](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/562d705673859548c58b46d8f2383ab8a053797f/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/constraints.py#L106-L110) before they are sent.

**Local reproduction.** Adding only the missing Pod mapping produced this failure for an illustrative uppercase rack label. It shows why the label's case must also survive serialization:

```text
assert manifest["spec"]["nodeSelector"]["ds.coreweave.com/nvlink.domain"] == rack
E AssertionError: assert 'dh1-001-us-east-08a' == 'DH1-001-US-EAST-08A'
```

The [draft PR's regression test](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/a30e700ae2cc164e28b8f244a8fe9a65f8584454/lib/iris/tests/cluster/backends/k8s/test_pod_manifest.py#L681-L693) checks that the exact label survives controller storage and reaches the Pod's selector and required affinity.

</details>

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖

# Research

`group_by="nvlink.domain"` keeps a gang in one NVLink domain but cannot name the rack; the Kubernetes backend renders only `pool` and `region` constraints as node selectors. `AttributeValue` lowercases strings, so the current constraint round trip loses the case of CoreWeave rack labels. A [prior rack-pinning incident](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/425) required temporary `iris.pool` labels to keep builds on an authorized rack.

**Relevant code**
- [`coreweave_topology.py#L58-L76`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/platforms/k8s/coreweave_topology.py#L58-L76) — gang topology levels
- [`constraints.py#L92-L103`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/constraints.py#L92-L103) — string normalization
- [`tasks.py#L154-L157`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py#L154-L157) — supported node selectors

# Proposed Fix

I recommend supporting an opt-in, required `nvlink.domain == <rack label>` constraint that preserves the label's case and adds both a Pod selector and required node affinity. [Kueue writes its assigned topology label into the selector](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kueue/blob/main/pkg/controller/tas/topology_ungater.go#L1888-L1902), and [Kubernetes requires selector and affinity together](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/assign-pod-node/#node-affinity), so the affinity retains the named-rack requirement after admission. [Draft PR #9478](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9478) implements this scope; review and a live placement check belong there. A missing or full rack leaves the job pending, and this constraint does not reserve training racks or resolve the Batch contention in [#8925](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8925).

spillover_issues.body:
On a developer VM in `us-west2`, a local artifact launch without `MARIN_PREFIX` resolves its output to `gs://marin-us-west2`. The Marin data configuration has no `us-west2` bucket. `StepRunner` then fails while it writes `.executor_info`, before it submits the remote job:

```
FileNotFoundError: https://storage.googleapis.com/upload/storage/v1/b/marin-us-west2/o?name=...%2F.executor_info
```

Reproduce:
1. Unset `MARIN_PREFIX` and use the default `MARIN_CLUSTER=marin` configuration on a host whose metadata region is `us-west2`.
2. Run `uv run python -c 'from rigging.filesystem.cluster_config import marin_prefix; print(marin_prefix())'` and observe `gs://marin-us-west2`.
3. Launch an artifact step and observe the failure before remote job submission.

Expected: storage resolution either selects a configured bucket or fails before launch with an error that names the unmapped region and the required prefix setting. It must not synthesize a bucket that is absent from the data configuration.

`DataConfig.resolved_root()` returns `{scheme}://marin-{region}` when instance metadata reports a region that is not in `region_buckets`. Issue #9528 uses `MARIN_PREFIX=s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin` as a temporary launch workaround.

comments.body:
🤖
# Research

Marin promotes an all-ungraded sample summary only when an aggregate graded count equals the attempted count; `task_item_count()` currently ignores `scored_count`. The pinned CRUXEval adapter writes `input_pass@1` and `output_pass@1` but no aggregate count, although its per-direction pass-rate maps identify the graded task IDs. Open PR #9461 already adds Marin's `scored_count` handling and a mismatch guard for HumanEval+/MBPP+.

**Relevant code**
- [`runner.py#L154-L179`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/4aa26ec73d248b974766f8940a896a8c888d8269/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evalchemy/runner.py#L154-L179) — count reconciliation
- [`eval_measurements.py#L75-L86`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/4aa26ec73d248b974766f8940a896a8c888d8269/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/eval_measurements.py#L75-L86) — recognized count keys
- [`eval_instruct.py#L265-L319`](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/blob/e3f4a3d601896c437f37b0bd0a30e51651cce6d0/eval/chat_benchmarks/CruxEval/eval_instruct.py#L265-L319) — CRUXEval scoring output
- [PR #9461](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9461) — overlapping Marin fix

# Proposed Fix

1. Use PR #9461 for HumanEval+/MBPP+ count recognition; avoid a duplicate Marin implementation.
2. In the Evalchemy fork, have `CruxEvalBenchmark.evaluate_responses()` emit `scored_count` from the number of task IDs in each completed `PER_TASK_PASS_RATE_FIELD` map, summed across input and output. A missing or partial direction must contribute only its graded IDs, never the dataset size.
3. Test full and partial CRUXEval results in the fork, pin that revision in Marin through `config/update-external.py`, and add a native FineStore regression: matching `scored_count` promotes coverage, while a smaller or conflicting count leaves the samples ungraded.

The existing Snowball record retains its aggregate scores but cannot establish graded coverage or sample-level uncertainty. New counts require a new run; CRUXEval's directional pass rates also need directional score statistics before claiming an uncertainty interval for either rate.

spillover_issues.author: Helw150
spillover_issues.body:
Hard benchmarks, especially agentic tasks, require large base models before downstream scores become useful. This makes a closed loop of pretraining, posttraining, and evaluation undoably expensive (even just the last two steps are expensive!). The goal is to assess whether hints on smaller models provide enough signal to guide SFT recipe improvements using extremely small proxy models.

Not set in stone, but seems reasonable to use [Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.09.21](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.09.21) as the larger, post-emergence checkpoint for validation.

## Starting points

- The new pretraining scaling ladder from Larry in https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9287
- The existing [hint-based estimation work](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/4549).
- The [evaluation policies](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9113).

## What this builds

Augment the new pretraining ladder with corresponding SFT path. Implements hint-assisted evaluation as reusable code that plugs into the existing evalchemy based evaluation tooling and the ladder. Start with hard, preferably agentic tasks, expanding to all tasks in the eval policy if there is time!

Assess how the hinted scores relate to unassisted performance on the larger checkpoint. Use that evidence to judge whether the method provides a useful signal for recipe selection.

Use hint-assisted scoring to develop and test a new SFT recipe expected to produce stronger results. Compare it with the initial recipe across the ladder and explain what the measurements support about its expected larger-scale performance.

What done looks like

- [ ] The pretraining ladder has corresponding SFT checkpoints, with reproducible training configurations.
- [ ] Hint-assisted evaluation is implemented and runs across the ladder, alongside unhinted baselines.
- [ ] The relationship between ladder scores and the larger checkpoint’s unassisted performance is measured and reported.
- [ ] Hint-assisted scores have informed at least one SFT recipe iteration, with a comparison against the initial recipe.
- [ ] A writeup assesses predictive value, uncertainty, accelerator cost, and whether the scoring method is useful for selecting SFT recipes.
- [ ] Code, configurations, and results are available to reproduce the experiments.

The outcome is an assessment of viability. Report failures and inconclusive results as well as improvements.

Out of scope

- RL.
- Changing the scaling ladder’s underlying training implementation.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

The likely ladder is the four-rung `experiments/grug/fast_track` MoE ladder tracked in [#9451](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451). Its published runs do not by default retain permanent checkpoints, and its 16k tokenizer and KDA/MLA architecture differ from the named [67B SFT checkpoint](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.09.21) (128k vocabulary, 256 experts). The prior [pass@k study](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/4549) establishes a hint/scaffold motivation, but its reported solution-primed GSM8K score saturated at pass@32; it does not establish that hints rank SFT recipes on hard agentic tasks. [#9537](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9537) has a one-example serving smoke test for the 67B checkpoint, while chat reasoning extraction remains untested. [#9348](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9348) studies student-guided SFT data selection, a related but distinct question; I found no open PR implementing this hint-evaluation study.

**Relevant code**
- [`fast_track/launch.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/4aa26ec73d248b974766f8940a896a8c888d8269/experiments/grug/fast_track/launch.py#L254-L269) — rung and checkpoint controls.
- [`fast_track/train.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/4aa26ec73d248b974766f8940a896a8c888d8269/experiments/grug/fast_track/train.py#L196-L217) — model-specific training data path.
- [`sft/launcher.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/4aa26ec73d248b974766f8940a896a8c888d8269/experiments/sft/launcher.py) — reusable SFT specification and chat masking.
- [`evaluation/README.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/4aa26ec73d248b974766f8940a896a8c888d8269/experiments/evaluation/README.md) — shared Evalchemy/Harbor launcher and records.

# Proposed Fix

1. **Freeze the comparison.** Inventory which d512/d768/d1024/d1280 pretraining checkpoints exist; rerun missing rungs with `--save-checkpoints`. Pin their commits, data, tokenizer, model configs, and checkpoint URIs. Choose one initial SFT recipe aligned with [#8089](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8089), including immutable data revisions, chat template, loss mask, step/token budget, seed, and export contract. Keep the pretraining ladder implementation unchanged.
2. **Make one rung end to end.** Adapt the `fast_track` model to the existing SFT data path, with a weights-only start and completion-token loss, then export and serve one d512 checkpoint. Verify unhinted evaluation and stored per-task samples before training all four rungs. Keep SFT/backend and serving changes in reviewable PRs separate from evaluation policy changes.
3. **Add versioned hints to the evaluation tooling.** Start with a fixed hard Harbor panel from the [current eval policy](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9409), such as TBLite/TB2 and SWE-bench Verified random-100. Define no-hint and at least two fixed hint strengths per task, record the hint source and text with each sample, and keep the agent, generation settings, verifier, task IDs, and attempt budget identical. Audit hints for answer leakage; add behavioral tests for hint injection and result identity. Extend to Evalchemy tasks only after the agentic pilot works.
4. **Run the matrix.** Evaluate the initial SFT recipe at all four rungs with and without hints, then choose one changed SFT recipe using a development task split and retrain all rungs at matched SFT compute. Score both recipes on held-out tasks with the same policy and seeds. Run the named 67B checkpoint unhinted on those tasks after chat-mode serving is verified. Publish run IDs, checkpoint/config revisions, per-task outcomes, failures, training GPU-hours, inference tokens/GPU-hours, and Harbor sandbox cost.
5. **Test predictive value.** On held-out tasks, compare hinted small-model scores with the 67B unhinted scores and with the cheaper small-model unhinted baseline. Report task-paired bootstrap intervals, rank agreement across rungs, recipe deltas, saturation, and cost per discriminating comparison. A single 67B recipe cannot validate a *recipe uplift* prediction at 67B; unless a matched second large-checkpoint recipe is available, report the larger-scale recipe conclusion as a hypothesis with that limitation explicit.

The first decision gate is an end-to-end d512 run: if checkpoint export/serving or non-leaking hints fail, resolve those before spending on the full ladder. Treat the 16k-to-128k tokenizer and architecture change as an external-validity limit even if the task-level correlations are positive.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

`SkyRLSpec.__post_init__` checks Marin's role plan and backend constraints, but never runs the selected MarinSkyRL parser. The rendered recipe reaches `MarinSkyRL.load_launch_config()` only in the launcher; at `fbfa158d`, that function calls `parse_rl_config()`, which rejects `terminal_bench.harbor.max_turns` when `context_budget` owns it. No open Marin PR covers this validation gap.

**Relevant code**
- [`skyrl.py#L366-L367`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/4aa26ec73d248b974766f8940a896a8c888d8269/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/skyrl.py#L366-L367) — local construction check
- [`skyrl.py#L566-L576`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/4aa26ec73d248b974766f8940a896a8c888d8269/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/skyrl.py#L566-L576) — Marin-only recipe validation
- [`skyrl.py#L812-L814`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/4aa26ec73d248b974766f8940a896a8c888d8269/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/skyrl.py#L812-L814) — recipe forwarded unchanged
- [`launch_config.py#L237-L245`](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/fbfa158d4caf7003d5fe64d58f4faf5c600ec156/cloud/iris/launch_config.py#L237-L245) — remote composition boundary
- [`rl_config_translation.py#L202-L208`](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/fbfa158d4caf7003d5fe64d58f4faf5c600ec156/cloud/iris/rl_config_translation.py#L202-L208) — derived-field rejection

# Proposed Fix

1. In MarinSkyRL, expose a CPU-only recipe-validation command that calls `parse_rl_config()` on the source YAML and returns its error unchanged. Keep this path free of Iris submission, artifact reads, training imports, and GPU dependencies; package it so Marin can install the parser at an exact commit without resolving the full training runtime.
2. Pin the revision containing that command in Marin. Call it during `SkyRLSpec` construction with `spec.runtime.commit`, before graph compilation can submit a coordinator. Cache successful validation by revision and recipe contents within the process, and fail the local build if the validator cannot run. Keep Marin's existing role-plan checks for its own contract.
3. Add a regression in `tests/rl/test_skyrl.py` using the reported `context_budget` plus `terminal_bench.harbor.max_turns` recipe. The local graph build must fail with the pinned parser's derived-field error and create no Iris job. A valid recipe with only `context_budget.max_turns` must build. Update existing synthetic recipe fixtures to satisfy the parser, then run the affected safe tests, required pre-commit checks, and the #9528 coding-expert smoke build before opening the Marin PR.

This needs an upstream validation/package surface and then a Marin integration PR. The pinned parser remains the validation authority for future revision-specific rules.

`shellbox.agent:BashAgent` sends Harbor's provider-qualified model name directly to the SkyRL OpenAI endpoint. Harbor supplies `hosted_vllm/<served-name>`, but the endpoint accepts `<served-name>`. The endpoint returns HTTP 400 before generation.

The Snowball coding-expert smoke in #9528 confirmed this on 40 H100s. Every observed four-sample batch completed with 0/4 successful trajectories and `HTTPStatusError: 400 Bad Request`. The run used MarinSkyRL `92fbe512` and Shellbox `c96bf413`.

The path is deterministic:

1. The MarinSkyRL Harbor runner creates `model_name="hosted_vllm/<served-name>"`.
2. Harbor `BaseAgent` keeps that value as `model_alias`.
3. `BashAgent.run()` sends `model_alias` as the JSON `model` field.
4. The SkyRL HTTP bridge compares it with the vLLM served name and rejects it.

LiteLLM agents remove the provider prefix before they send the request. `BashAgent` owns its HTTP loop and does not perform that step.

Normalize Harbor's `hosted_vllm/` provider form before a direct OpenAI request. Preserve model names that do not use that provider form. Include the response body in request failure details so a future endpoint rejection is diagnosable.

The temporary workaround for #9528 strips the known prefix in `BashAgent` before the request. A focused test must cover the exact payload sent to the endpoint.

spillover_issues.author: ravwojdyla-agent
spillover_issues.body:
`shellbox.agent:BashAgent` accepts unknown Harbor agent arguments through `**kwargs`, but it does not apply `llm_call_kwargs` to its direct OpenAI request. MarinSkyRL derives `llm_call_kwargs.max_tokens` from `context_budget.max_new_tokens_per_turn`, so the configured 4,096-token turn limit is lost.

The request body currently contains `extra_body`, `model`, `messages`, and `tools`. It does not contain `max_tokens`. This is visible from the code path used by the live Snowball coding-expert smoke in #9528. HTTP 400 model-name failures occurred first, so the live run did not reach generation and cannot measure the resulting response length.

Accept `llm_call_kwargs` explicitly and merge it into each direct OpenAI request. Keep `model`, `messages`, and `tools` controlled by `BashAgent`. A focused HTTP test must show that `max_tokens` and `extra_body` both reach the endpoint.

The temporary workaround for #9528 adds that request mapping before the next smoke.

spillover_issues.author: ravwojdyla-agent
spillover_issues.body:
`ShellSimEnvironment.download_dir()` converts its target with `pathlib.Path`. Harbor can supply a remote `S3Path` for a trial log directory. `Path(S3Path(...))` raises `TypeError`, so Harbor cannot collect agent logs after a trial error.

The Snowball coding-expert smoke in #9528 confirmed this after the agent endpoint returned HTTP 400:

```text
File "shellbox/backends/shellsim/environment.py", line 146, in download_dir
    target = Path(target_dir)
TypeError: argument should be a str or an os.PathLike object where __fspath__ returns a str, not 'S3Path'
```

This secondary failure removes the useful agent log and makes the first failure harder to diagnose.

Support Harbor's remote path objects in `download_file()` and `download_dir()`. Download from ShellSim to a local temporary path, then copy the result to the remote target. Keep the current direct path for local targets.

The temporary workaround for #9528 implements this staging path in Shellbox. Tests must cover a non-`pathlib.Path` target without access to live object storage.

`shellbox.agent:BashAgent` ends a complete Harbor trial when the model emits a tool name other than the declared `Bash` function.

The Snowball Python expert smoke reached real rollout generation after the model-alias fix. Several independent trajectories then failed at `shellbox/agent.py:176` with names such as `WriteFile`, `write`, `Dir`, `mkdir`, and `SetStackTraceLineAnalyzer`. One batch completed 4/4, while another completed 3/4 because one unsupported call ended its trial. This converts one recoverable model action into an infrastructure-style trajectory failure and loses the remaining turn budget.

Keep the trial alive. Return a structured tool result that says that the name is unsupported and that `Bash` is the available tool. The model can then correct its next action within the existing turn limit. Do not execute an undeclared tool or map arbitrary names to shell commands.

Update `BashAgent` to append a tool response for unsupported names and continue. Extend the complete Harbor and ShellSim smoke so a fake model first calls `WriteFile`, receives the structured error, then calls `Bash` and passes the verifier.

This preserves the one-tool security boundary and makes model mistakes part of the recorded trajectory.

spillover_issues.author: ClassicLarry
spillover_issues.body:
This issue tracks iterative improvements to the Marin pretraining scaling ladder (`experiments/grug/fast_track`) using the **Marin Belay** process. It is a twist on autoresearch: an agent runs experiments in batches, and anyone can steer it with research directions. > **To suggest a research direction, comment on [Marin Belay Intake (#9514)](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9514).** Suggestions a maintainer approves (👍 from a `marin-devs` member) are copied into this thread automatically, and the agent acts only on this thread. This thread holds the agent's batch reports and maintainer steering. ![fast_track MoE ladder: Marin 535B baseline vs clean KMA](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/a2ff0a17aff9c4483e4715340444515bfafa3c1c/v1/ladder_scaling.png) The Marin 535B compute-optimal baseline follows `L(C) = 1.2 + 59.0·C^(−0.0843)` over four data-matched rungs. Clean KMA, the current baseline (★), is 0.022 lower at d512, 0.049 lower at d768, 0.040 lower at d1024 and 0.033 lower at d1280, which is about 1.14×, 1.43×, 1.40× and 1.35× the baseline's compute efficiency. Its dashed curve is fit to all four points: `L(C) = 1.2 + 64.8·C^(−0.0870)`. The **?** marks the open question this issue is chasing: how much further down each point can go. The right panel is clean KMA's training MFU at each rung on one 8×H100 node: 9.5% at d512 and d768, 12.2% at d1024, and 13.0% at d1280. FLOPs are counted from KMA's own layers (KDA, MLA + Inkling, AttnRes), as 3× forward with no recompute. The trainer's logged `throughput/mfu` uses the baseline architecture's FLOP formula, so it is slightly off for KMA. ## Objective **Minimize Paloma macro loss (`eval/paloma/macro_loss`, final step) at the d512 rung after a fixed 8 minutes of 8×H100 train-step time.** - **Fixed time, not fixed tokens.** Faster code trains on more tokens within the 8 minutes, so a pure speedup counts as a win. - The LR schedule depends on the step count, so fix steps before each run: `num_steps = round(480 s × ex/s ÷ batch)`. - Measure ex/s with a short `--no-eval` probe (~30 steps) on the same cluster, and use the steady-state throughput. - Compile, evals and startup are excluded from the 8 minutes. - **Numerics changes are allowed** (e.g. FP8, precision changes, approximate kernels). They count as ordinary wins; no parity check needed. - **Noise.** Differences under ~0.005 are noise. A win must beat the current best by more than 0.005. ### Gates (both relative to the current baseline, same fixed-time rule at each rung) - **Gate 1:** beat the baseline at d512 and d768. - **Gate 2:** also beat it at d1024 and d1280, **and** project to lower Paloma macro loss at 1e24 FLOPs. Fit a power law of final loss against training FLOPs across the four rungs, for both the baseline and the variant, fixing the asymptote to 1.2. ### Fixed - Training data, the 16k BPE tokenizer, and the eval sets. - Sequence length 4096. - One 8×H100 node per rung. - The FLOP accounting used for the gate-2 projection. ### Judgment calls - **Hero-scale speed is out of scope for v1, so use discretion.** - Robust target criteria would also check training speed and inference speed at hero scale. Marin Belay v1 skips those checks. - Judge whether a change's d512 gain would carry over to hero scale, and avoid changes whose gain comes from d512-only effects. Two examples: - Dropping MoE for dense would be a clear win at d512 because dense gets ~5× higher MFU there, but that MFU gain would not carry over at hero scale. - A much larger KV cache would also be a clear win at d512, but it would hurt long-context inference speed. - **Avoid magic numbers.** - Prefer changes with few new tuned constants. A tuned constant is justified when its gain is above the noise threshold and holds as a pattern across scales. For example, a 2× LR on one parameter group qualifies if it clears the noise threshold and the gain shows up consistently at larger rungs. - The higher a change's risk of curve fitting, the more scales it must be validated at before it counts as a win. - **Spend effort in proportion to an idea's likelihood of improvement.** - Promising ideas deserve several attempts. Long shots can be tried once and dropped. - A first run is not a verdict for a large change. If you try a new architecture or component, tune its optimizer assignment, LR, init and other key hyperparameters before concluding it doesn't work. The baseline's settings were tuned for the baseline, not for the new idea. ## Architecture (current best, d512) The diagrams below show **clean KMA**. The current best recipe adds the components listed under **Status → Current best recipe**: MLA key norm and key offset, a gated bigram-memory AttnRes source, ReLU² experts, and optimizer, schedule and logit changes. The diagrams show d512; the other rungs differ in the Shape table only. **1. Layer stack and Block Attention Residuals.** Every sublayer reads its input through its own AttnRes gate, a per-token softmax over the residual history. At d512 each layer closes an AttnRes block, so the history at layer *i* is the embedding plus one sum per earlier layer. [¹](#arch-note) ```mermaid flowchart TB tok["token ids
B × 4096, packed documents"] --> emb["token embedding
16384 × 512"] emb --> en["RMSNorm → GatedNorm"] en --> S0(["source 0
embedding"]) S0 --> L0 subgraph STACK["6 layers: local KDA ×4, global MLA ×2 (every 4th + last)"] direction TB L0["layer 0 · KDA + MoE"] --> L1["layer 1 · KDA + MoE"] --> L2["layer 2 · KDA + MoE"] L2 --> L3["layer 3 · MLA + Inkling + MoE"] --> L4["layer 4 · KDA + MoE"] --> L5["layer 5 · MLA + Inkling + MoE"] end L0 -. "block sum b0" .-> H L1 -. "b1" .-> H L2 -. "b2" .-> H L3 -. "b3" .-> H L4 -. "b4" .-> H S0 -.-> H H[("AttnRes history, read by every gate

fused CE, vocab tile 8192, z-loss 1e-4"] head --> loss(["next-token loss"]) ``` **2. One layer.** The two sublayers each have an AttnRes gate. The MoE gate also sees the attention output written just before it, as the running partial. ```mermaid flowchart TB Hin[("history

Inkling bias added before softmax"] fa --> xsa["XSA: subtract each head's component along its own v"] --> mg["× 2σ(x W_gate), per head, zero-init"] --> mo["W_o → ShortConv → sublayer out"] ``` **3c. LatentMoE with quantile-balanced routing (every layer).** ```mermaid flowchart TB ex["x (512)"] --> fused["one fused GEMM:
router · W_latent↓ · shared-expert gate/up"] fused --> rt["router logits (fp32)
top-(8+1) on logit − β_QB; 9th = threshold α"] rt --> qb["QB: β_e = global (1 − 8/384) quantile of logit − α
10k-bin histogram each step; router bias = −β, not trained"] rt --> cw["combine weights = σ(unbiased logits) of the top 8,
renormalized to sum to 2.5"] fused --> lat["latent = RMSNorm(x W_latent↓), 256 wide"] lat & cw --> ep["384 SwiGLU experts, hidden 256
pooled-wave EP all-to-all over 8 GPUs, capacity 1.15"] ep --> up["W_latent↑ 256 → 512"] fused --> sh["2 shared SwiGLU experts, 512 → 256 → 512
down projections fused into one GEMM"] up & sh --> sum["routed + shared → ShortConv → sublayer out"] ``` ¹ AttnRes rolls a new block at layer *i* while `i % max(1, L // 8) == 0` and fewer than 8 blocks exist. At d512 and d768 every layer closes a block. At d1024 (12 layers) and d1280 (14 layers) only layers 0–7 do, so layers 8 and up all accumulate into one running partial instead of their own blocks. **Optimizer routing:** - **MuonH:** every attention and MoE matrix, and every GatedNorm (KDA `W_β` at 2× the MuonH LR). - **AdamH:** lm_head. - **Adam:** embedding, router, attention output gate, norm gains, ShortConv kernels, KDA decay parameters, Inkling weights. - **Adam at 0.1× the Adam LR:** the AttnRes queries. ## Baseline: clean KMA Branch [`fasttrack-moe-kma`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/fasttrack-moe-kma) @ `4eba59cafa`. Build from this branch. The recipe below covers every model and optimizer component. Values are for d512 unless noted; the code is `experiments/grug/fast_track/{model,optimizer,heuristic,launch}.py`. **Shape** | Rung | Width D | Layers | Local (KDA) / global (MLA) layers | Heads × head dim | Batch | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | d512 | 512 | 6 | 4 / 2 | 4 × 128 | 128 | | d768 | 768 | 8 | 6 / 2 | 6 × 128 | 128 | | d1024 | 1024 | 12 | 9 / 3 | 8 × 128 | 256 | | d1280 | 1280 | 14 | 10 / 4 | 10 × 128 | 256 | - Every 4th layer and the last layer are global; all other layers are local. - The run uses a 16k vocab and sequence length 4096 with packed documents. Every ShortConv and the KDA state respect document boundaries (the KDA state resets at each document start). - Weights are initialized with std 0.5/√D. Compute is bf16. **Embedding and output** - Token embedding → RMSNorm → GatedNorm. The result is AttnRes source 0. - Output path: final AttnRes gate → RMSNorm → GatedNorm → untied lm_head (`output_proj`). - The fused lm_head + cross-entropy loop uses a vocab tile of 8192. - GatedNorm (every GatedNorm in the model) is `x · sigmoid(W_up · SiLU(W_down · x))`, with a rank-128 bottleneck. **Block (every layer)** - **Attention sublayer:** input = its AttnRes gate mix → RMSNorm → GatedNorm → mixer (KDA or MLA). - **MoE sublayer:** input = its AttnRes gate mix → RMSNorm → GatedNorm → MoE → ShortConv on the MoE output. - Each ShortConv is a 4-tap causal depthwise conv. **Local layers: Kimi Delta Attention** (Kimi K3's layer) - **Projections:** q/k/v are D → N·128 with full heads (no GQA). Each goes through a ShortConv followed by SiLU. q and k are L2-normalized, and q is scaled by 1/√128. - **Decay:** per-channel log-decay `g = −5·sigmoid(exp(A_log)·(x·W_a_down·W_a_up + dt_bias))`. - The gate projection has rank 128. - `A_log` is one value per head, initialized to 0. - `dt_bias` is one value per channel, initialized so the decay rate spans 0.02–0.5. - **Write strength:** `β = sigmoid(x·W_β)`, one value per head. - **Recurrence:** `S_t = (I − β·k·kᵀ)·Diag(exp(g))·S_{t−1} + β·k·vᵀ`, read out as `o_t = S_tᵀ·q_t`. - It runs as chunked Pallas kernels, with a stable block-doubling inverse inside each chunk. - **Output:** per-head RMSNorm with a learnable 128-wide scale shared across heads → full-rank per-channel gate `sigmoid(x·W_g)` → `W_o`. - No positional encoding, no window, no XSA, and no ShortConv on the branch output. **Global layers: MLA + Inkling relative position** - **q:** full-rank, D → N·128 (no Q latent). - **k and v:** k = `W_uk · RMSNorm(x·W_dkv)` and v = `W_uv · RMSNorm(x·W_dkv)`. - They share one 512-wide KV latent, with a learnable RMSNorm on the latent. - Heads are 128 wide with no RoPE part. - There's no ShortConv on K, so the up-projections can be absorbed at inference. - **Scaling:** no QK-norm; `qk_mult` = 1, i.e. standard 1/√128 logit scaling. - **Position — Inkling relative-position bias**, added to the pre-softmax logits in place of RoPE: - `bias[h,i,j] = R[i,h,:] · P[:, i−j]`, where `R = x·W_r` is 16 values per head. - `P` is a bank of shape [16 × 1024] shared across heads. The relative extent is 1024. - It runs inside the FA4 attention kernel (forward, backward, and the SM90 backward pass). - **XSA** (exclusive self-attention): subtract the component of each head's output that is parallel to its own value vector. - **Output gate:** per head, `2·sigmoid(x·W_gate)`. `W_gate` is zero-initialized, so the gate is 1 at init. - The branch output also gets a ShortConv. **MoE sublayer (LatentMoE with quantile-balanced routing)** - **Experts:** 384 routed experts, top-8. Each is a SwiGLU with hidden size D/2. - **Latent space:** experts operate in a D/2-wide latent. The input goes through `W_latent_down` → RMSNorm, and the combined expert output goes back up through `W_latent_up`. - **Router:** reads the full-width token and computes logits in fp32. - Experts are selected by top-(8+1) on bias-adjusted logits, where the 9th logit is the threshold α. - Combine weights are the sigmoid of the unbiased logits, renormalized to sum to 2.5. - **Quantile balancing:** each step, each expert's threshold β is the global (1 − K/E) quantile of the logit margins (logit − α), read from a 10k-bin histogram. The router bias is set to −β. - The router bias is not trained by gradient. - **Capacity:** capacity factor 1.15, with pooled-wave expert-parallel dispatch. Receiver ranks are sort-based and the expand backward is gather-based. - **Shared experts:** 2 shared SwiGLU experts that bypass the latent: D → D/2 hidden → D. - **Fused projections:** - The router, latent-down, and both shared experts' gate/up projections run as one GEMM. - The shared experts' down-projections run as one GEMM. **Residual stream: Block Attention Residuals** - **Sources:** the embedding source, one running sum per completed block of sublayer outputs, and the running partial sum of the current block. - The model has 8 blocks. Block sums use the raw sublayer outputs. - **Gates:** every sublayer (attention and MoE) has its own gate, and there is one final gate before the output norm. Each gate has one learned pseudo-query `q ∈ ℝᴰ`, zero-initialized so every gate starts as a uniform average. - **Mixing:** per token, `logitᵢ = q · rms_norm(sourceᵢ)`, using a parameter-free (frozen) RMS key norm, then `softmax` over sources and a weighted sum of the raw sources. - **Implementation:** - Each completed block is scored once against every gate that reads it. - Backward: at d512 the layer's forward intermediates are saved. At d768–d1280 each layer is recomputed. At d1280 the attention branch is also rematerialized. - The model keeps one layer stack per mixer kind. **Optimizer** | Group | Update rule | LR | Parameters | |---|---|---|---| | `muonh` | MuonH | MuonH LR | all attention and MoE matrices: MLA `W_q`/`W_dkv`/`W_uk`/`W_uv`/`W_o`; KDA `W_q`/`W_k`/`W_v`/`W_o`/`W_g`; experts; shared experts; latent down/up. Also every GatedNorm `W_down`/`W_up`. | | `kda_beta` | MuonH | 2 × MuonH LR | KDA `W_β` | | `adamh` | AdamH | MuonH LR | lm_head (`output_proj`) | | `adam` | Adam | Adam LR | token embedding; router; attention output gate; router bias slot (overwritten by QB); all 1-D norm gains; ShortConv kernels; KDA `W_a_down`/`W_a_up`, `A_log`, `dt_bias`; Inkling `W_r` and `P` | | `attn_res_query` | Adam | 0.1 × Adam LR | the AttnRes pseudo-queries | - **MuonH:** Nesterov momentum 0.95 → Newton–Schulz orthogonalization (5 quintic steps, bucketed across same-shape matrices) → a step along that direction, then projection back onto the matrix's Frobenius sphere. Each matrix's norm stays fixed at its init value. - **AdamH:** the Adam direction with the same Frobenius-sphere (hyperball) projection. - **Adam:** β1 0.9. Only the router and the attention output gate get decoupled weight decay (0.02). No other parameter gets weight decay, and there's no gradient clipping. - **Schedule:** 1% warmup, then linear decay to 0.05× peak. - **Peak values** from `MoeHeuristic` (they depend on tokens, width and batch): - Adam LR = `0.0876 · tokens^−0.346 · D^−0.345 · √(tokens per batch)`. - MuonH LR = 13/3 × Adam LR. - β2 = `0.999^(tokens per batch / 131072)`. - ε = `9.68e−18 · √(steps)`. - At d512 with 2384 steps: MuonH LR 0.0227, Adam LR 0.0052, β2 0.996, ε 4.7e−16. Submit (the default priority is interactive): ``` NO_PROXY="*" uv run python -m experiments.grug.fast_track.launch --submit \ --target-cluster cw-us-east-02a --priority interactive \ --run-id --size d512 --recipe kma --num-steps <8-min steps> --version ``` ## Compute - cw-us-east-02a at **interactive** priority. - **At most 10 active runs at once**, probes included. - **Limit runs above d768** to keep the experimentation rate high. d1024 and d1280 runs take hours and hold a slot the whole time, so save them for changes that have already passed gate 1 or that need extra scales because of curve-fitting risk. - Don't save checkpoints (the launcher default). ## For humans Comment with a research direction for the agent, for example "try X", or "combine A and B". The agent picks up new comments at its next batch. The main goal of a single experiment should be to learn about the system. This means that if you tweak one knob and the loss goes off the rails, the experiment can still be considered a success! We better understand the system sensitivity! Building knowledge through failed experiments will bring us closer to the long term goal of better models. ## For the agent - Read `experiments/grug/fast_track/README.md` and `agent.md` first. Where they differ from this issue, this issue wins; the main difference is the fixed-time objective. - Run 5–10 experiments per batch, and prioritize human comments when picking the next one. - Ask for clarification in the thread if helpful, but never hold a batch waiting for an answer: state your assumption and correct it in the next batch. - Start at d512. When a change beats the current best by more than 0.005, validate it at d768. - Post **one comment per batch** and edit it as runs finish. Start it with 🤖 and include: - the batch goal, and which human comments it addresses; - a table with one row per run: change | branch@commit | W&B link | steps | ex/s | mid loss | final Paloma macro loss | Δ vs current best; - a 1–3 line takeaway and the planned next batch. - **Branches:** prefix with `ladderclimb_v1_`, and link the exact commit each job ran. - **W&B:** project `marin_moe`, with short prefixed run IDs such as `lc1-b03-…` (names over 128 characters fail at init). - Add the `agent-generated` label to any issue or PR you open. - Keep the **Status** table below updated with a concise chronology of improvements. ## Status ### Current best recipe (d512): candidate 9 **At equal steps (2817): 2.9750 / 2.9791** (seeds 0 / 1, 185–187 ms median step), i.e. **k ≈ 2.52× vs clean KMA**. comments.body:
Some ideas to get started. Treat this as a general pool of ideas, that indicates the spirit of what can be tried.
1. https://blog.tilderesearch.com/blog/online-kl-shampoo. Consider interactions with hyperball and selectively replace matrices.
2. Add a second embedding table with its own random init. Attn residuals queries both embedding tables, treating them as unique inputs.
3. Lets add value embeddings. That is, a second embedding table that gets added to V on the MLA layers. So take KV latent-> project to num_heads of size 128. Then do values = lambda1*values + lambda2*value_embeds[layer_i]. lambda 1 init to 1, lambda2 init to 0. value_embeds has [vocab_size, num_heads*head_dim, num_mla_layers] dimension. Can also try gated value embeds, where instead of lambda2, its conditional on residual stream via sigmoid(linear(x)).
4. Add learnable scalars to each submodule output, that feeds into attention residuals. May be worth tracking and plotting these in wandb, to see if indicates any architecture changes will help.
5. Try different variations of linear attention to replace KDA.
6. It has been shown in many places that the final couple layers of attention dont prefer to attend to outputs from the final MLPs. See if there is any change to attention residuals to help make this more natural.
7. Adding an lm_head auxillary loss to the output of layer 1 for the first X (say 500) steps can help give the routed experts a cleaner role early. Unclear how this interacts with attention residuals.
8. Hash routing on first layer.
9. Instead of Adam/AdamH on embed and lm_head, look into other optimizers here that have shown promise in literature.
10. Do any weights benefit from extremely different beta1/beta2/momentum terms, or swapping their optimizer group.
11. Update the router behavior (sigmoid vs softmax), normalizing over picked experts vs not, sampling over experts instead of top k).
12. Null routing (enable tokens to select null experts which skips their computation, dynamic compute per token).
13. Multi-token-prediction.
14. Sparse attention.

If users give comments with singular specific ideas, give it priority over this laundry list.

🤖 **Batch 1: cheap architecture adds from the idea list, an LR check, and a noise and profile baseline** (d512, 2475 steps) — **done**

**Goal.** Test the lowest-cost ideas from @ClassicLarry's list: `#2` (second embedding table), `#3` (value embeddings, both forms), and `#4` (learnable sublayer output scalars, logged to W&B). Also check whether the `MoeHeuristic` LR, which was fit on the old baseline architecture, is still right for KMA (×1.5 and ×0.67 on both LRs). Add a seed-1 baseline to calibrate noise, and a 60-step profile to find speed levers. Speed counts as a win under the fixed-time objective.

**Assumption (I'll correct it next batch if it's wrong).** None of these changes adds meaningful compute, so all runs use the baseline's 2475 steps instead of a separate probe. After each run I check its steady-state ex/s. If it is more than about 1% below 660, I rerun at `round(480 × ex/s / 128)` steps. Branch [`ladderclimb_v1_batch01`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/eb26f3cbc9) @ `eb26f3cbc9`: every change is gated by a `--model-set` / `--opt-set` flag and defaults to off.

**Implementation details**
- **ve:** each MLA layer gets a [16384 × N·128] table, and `v = λ1·v + λ2·VE[token]` (λ1 = 1, λ2 = 0 at init). The tables, λ and the gate go to Adam at the Adam LR, like `token_embed`.
- **veg:** `v = λ1·v + sigmoid(x·W)·VE[token]`, with one gate per head. `W` is zero-initialized, so the gate starts at 0.5.
- **osc:** a scalar initialized to 1 on each attention and MoE sublayer output before it enters the AttnRes history (Adam). Logged as `train/attn_res/scale_{attn,mlp}_L*`.
- **emb2:** a second randomly initialized table → learnable RMSNorm, prepended as an extra AttnRes block that every gate can read.
